Monoidal Kleisli bicategories and the arithmetic product of coloured symmetric sequences
Nicola Gambino, Richard Garner, Christina Vasilakopoulou

Abstract
. We extend the arithmetic product of species of structures and symmetric sequences studied by Maia and Méndez and by Dwyer and Hess to coloured symmetric sequences and show that it determines a normal oplax monoidal structure on the bicategory of coloured symmetric sequences. In order to do this, we establish general results on extending monoidal structures to Kleisli bicategories. Our approach uses monoidal double categories, which help us to attack the difficult problem of verifying the coherence conditions for a monoidal bicategory in an efficient way.



.

2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
18N10, 18N15, 18M80, 18C20, 18M05

1.
Introduction

Context, aim and motivation

Joyal’s theory of species of structures
[
Joy81
]
provides an illuminating and powerful approach to enumerative combinatorics, as amply illustrated in
[
BLL98
]
, and finds applications also
in algebra
[
AM10
]
.
By definition, a species of structures
F
is simply a functor from the category
\mathfrak{B}
of finite sets and bijections to the category of sets and functions, mapping a finite set
U
of ‘labels’ to a set
F[U]
of ‘
F
-structures’ (
e.g.
binary rooted trees) labelled by elements of
U
.
Importantly for applications, species of structures support a calculus of operations (which includes substitution, sum, product and differentiation) that has a combinatorial interpretation and provides a ‘categorification’ of the calculus of exponential power series widely used in combinatorics
[
Wil06
]
. This point of view is supported by the introduction of
the so-called analytic functor associated to a species of structures
[
Joy86
]
, which is defined by the formula

F(X)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\frac{F[n]\times X^{n}}{\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\mathrlap{,}

where, for
n\in\mathbb{N}
,
[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}
and the fraction denotes the quotient of
F[n]\times X^{n}
by
the evident action of the
n
-th symmetric group
\mathfrak{S}_{n}
.
The passage from species of structures to analytic functors goes via
symmetric sequences, which are defined as functors from
\mathfrak{S}
, the skeleton of
\mathfrak{B}
whose objects are finite cardinals, into the category of sets.
Under the equivalence between species of structures and symmetric sequences, the substitution operation of species of structures corresponds to the substitution monoidal structure on symmetric sequences defined
in
[
Kel05
]
, which is of interest since monoids with respect to it are precisely symmetric operads
[
BV73
,
May72
]
.

In
[
MM08
]
, Maia and Méndez introduced a new operation on species of structures, baptized
arithmetic product
, and provided a combinatorial interpretation for it. Given species
F
and
G
, their arithmetic product
F\boxtimes G
is defined by letting

(F_{1}\boxtimes F_{2})[U]=\sum_{(\pi_{1},\pi_{2})\in\mathcal{R}[U]}F_{1}[\pi_{1}]\times F_{2}[\pi_{2}]\mathrlap{,}

where
\mathcal{R}[U]
denotes a certain set of partitions of
U
, called rectangles.
Independently of the work of Maia and Méndez, Dwyer and Hess rediscovered
this operation
1
1

1

Dwyer and Hess called it matrix multiplication. Here we prefer to say arithmetic product in order to
avoid potential confusion with the composition operation of the bicategory of matrices.
in the context of symmetric sequences
[
DH14
]

in order to extend the Boardman–Vogt tensor product of symmetric operads
[
BV73
]
to operadic bimodules. For symmetric sequences, the
arithmetic product is defined from the product of natural numbers on
\mathfrak{S}
(which is functorial, even if it is not the cartesian product) by Day
convolution
[
Day70
]
, via the coend formula

(1)

(F_{1}\boxtimes F_{2})[m]=\int^{m_{1},m_{2}}\mathfrak{S}[m,m_{1}\cdot m_{2}]\times F_{1}[m_{1}]\times F_{2}[m_{2}]\mathrlap{.}

The connection between the arithmetic product for species in
[
MM08
]
and symmetric sequences in
[
DH14
]
seems to
have been first noted by Bremner and Dotsenko in
[
BD20
]
.

In
[
DH14
]
, the authors also observed that the arithmetic product of symmetric sequences interacts with the substitution monoidal
structure in an interesting way, in that there is a natural transformation with components

(2)

(G_{1}\circ F_{1})\boxtimes(G_{2}\circ F_{2})\to(G_{1}\boxtimes G_{2})\circ(F_{1}\boxtimes F_{2})

which are not necessarily invertible.
Dwyer and Hess conjectured that this transformation underlies what is usually called a
duoidal
or
2-monoidal
structure, in which two
monoidal structures interact by means of an interchange law
[
AM10
]
. The conjecture was settled positively by the second-named author and
López Franco, who also showed that this duoidal structure is
normal
, in the sense that the units of the two monoidal structures essentially
coincide. This was done as part of their general study of commutative operations
[
GL16
]
, which involves introducing a general notion
of
commuting tensor product
of
\circ
-monoids in a normal duoidal category
(\mathcal{V},\mathord{\boxtimes},\circ)
. When this notion is
instantiated at the normal duoidal category of symmetric sequences, it re-finds the Boardman–Vogt tensor product
P\otimes_{\mathrm{BV}}Q
of
symmetric operads
P
and
Q
. In particular, to express that the operations of
P
and
Q

commute
with each other in
P\otimes_{\mathrm{BV}}Q
one uses a diagram of the form

(3)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P\boxtimes Q}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(P\otimes_{\mathrm{BV}}Q)\circ(P\otimes_{\mathrm{BV}}Q)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P\otimes_{\mathrm{BV}}Q}

which involves both the arithmetic product and the substitution monoidal structures.
Furthermore,
[
FV20
]
uses this duoidal structure to establish an enrichment of symmetric operads in symmetric cooperads.

The aim of this paper is to generalise the definition of the arithmetic product, and the key results concerning it, from symmetric sequences to
coloured symmetric sequences: this corresponds to the passage from symmetric operads to coloured symmetric operads,
i.e.
from the
single-object to the many-object case. We will show that such generalisation not only is possible, but actually
determines a new kind of low-dimensional categorical structure.

The motivation for this work is manifold. First, it is part of a wider research programme aimed at understanding the structure of the bicategory of coloured symmetric sequences and related bicategories, with applications to logic and theoretical computer science,
cf.

[
CW05
,
Hyl10
]
. In particular, it provides the basis to extend the Garner–López Franco theory of commutativity, to re-find the Boardman–Vogt tensor product of coloured symmetric operads (
cf.
(
3
)), and to develop a corresponding tensor product of bimodules between them, generalising the results of Dwyer and Hess, a project that we leave for future work. The results presented here are also useful to extend the study of enrichment in
[
Vas19
]
to relate coloured (co)operads and their (co)modules. Finally, we hope that
our results may eventually be of interest in combinatorics, since the arithmetic product of coloured symmetric sequences defined here
induces a corresponding operation on coloured species of structures
[
FGHW08
]
, which extends the arithmetic product of Maia and Méndez to variants of Joyal’s species of structures that are particular instances of coloured species of structures.

Main results

Whereas the original arithmetic product is extra structure on the substitution monoidal category of symmetric sequences, our generalised arithmetic
product for coloured symmetric
sequences will be extra structure on the bicategory
\mathsf{Sym}
of coloured symmetric sequences
of
[
FGHW08
]
.
Recall that, for sets
X
and
Y
, an
(X,Y)
-coloured symmetric sequence is a functor
M\colon SY^{\mathrm{op}}\times X\to\mathsf{Set}
,
where
SY
is the free symmetric strict monoidal category on
Y
.
Such a functor
M
assigns a set
M(\vec{y},x)
to each
\vec{y}=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{n})\in SY
and
x\in X
, the elements of which can be
thought of as operations
f\colon y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}\to x
, with inputs of sorts
y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}
and output of sort
x
, typically pictured as
corollas. Taking
X=Y=1
recovers the notion of ordinary symmetric sequence since
S1=\mathfrak{S}
; and as shown
in
[
Fio05
,
FGHW08
]
, the calculus of symmetric sequences can be extended to their coloured counterparts. In particular, the
substitution monoidal structure can be generalised to a composition operation, which is the composition of the bicategory
\mathsf{Sym}
whose objects
are sets, and whose maps from
X
to
Y
are the symmetric
(X,Y)
-coloured sequences
[
FGHW08
,
FGHW18
]
. The monads in this
bicategory are then symmetric coloured operads
[
BD98
]
.

Given an

(X_{1},Y_{1})
-coloured symmetric sequence

M
and a
(X_{2},Y_{2})
-coloured symmetric sequence
M_{2}
, we will define their arithmetic product as the
(X_{1}\times X_{2},Y_{1}\times Y_{2})
-coloured symmetric sequence
M_{1}\boxtimes M_{2}
given by

(4)

(M_{1}\boxtimes M_{2})(\vec{y},(x_{1},x_{2}))=\int^{\vec{y}^{1},\vec{y}^{2}\in SY}S(Y_{1}\times Y_{2})[\vec{y},\vec{y}_{1}\boxtimes\vec{y}_{2}]\times M_{1}(\vec{y}_{1},x_{1})\times M_{2}(\vec{y}_{2},x_{2})\mathrlap{,}

where

(5)

\boxtimes\colon SY_{1}\times SY_{2}\to S(Y_{1}\times Y_{2})

is an operation determined by lexicographic ordering of pairs.
As expected, when
X_{1}=Y_{1}=X_{2}=Y_{2}=1
, we obtain the arithmetic product in (
1
) of Dwyer and Hess.

Our main result,
10.10
, asserts that the said arithmetic product determines a
normal oplax monoidal structure
on the bicategory

\mathsf{Sym}
of coloured symmetric sequences. The notion of a normal oplax monoidal bicategory appears to be novel and is introduced here
in
4.9
as the natural ‘many-object’ generalisation of the normal duoidal structure in (
2
).
The key challenge to be overcome to obtain our main result is the verification of the axioms for a normal oplax monoidal bicategory, which are of the same daunting complexity as those for a monoidal bicategory
[
GPS95
,
Gur13
]
. As such, attempting a direct verification seems hopelessly
complicated and unlikely to result in any insight. Instead, we solve the problem developing ideas of 2-dimensional monad theory
[
BKP89
]
, obtaining some general results that are of independent interest.

Our approach exploits crucially the notion of a (pseudo) double category, which adeptly handles the bookwork around dealing with structures involving two kinds
of morphisms. More specifically, in a double category one has objects, two kinds of 1-cells (called horizontal and vertical), and squares (which help
to relate horizontal and vertical 1-cells).
Of key importance for our development are the double category of profunctors
\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}
, which has categories as objects,
profunctors
[
Bén73
,
Bén00
]
(also known as distributors or bimodules) as horizontal 1-cells and
functors as vertical 1-cells; and the double category of matrices
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}
, which is the full double subcategory of
\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}
spanned by sets (viewed as
discrete categories).

Double categories are important for us because they provide an efficient way of constructing three-dimensional structures such as monoidal
bicategories and, as we shall see, their oplax variants. The basic insight, as explained
in
[
GG09
,
Shu10
,
HS19
]
, is that, in order to obtain a monoidal structure on a bicategory
\mathcal{E}
, it
is sufficient to represent
\mathcal{E}
as the horizontal bicategory of a double category and then construct a monoidal structure on
this double category. Since the coherence data and axioms for a monoidal double category are of the same character as those of a monoidal category, rather than a monoidal bicategory, this significantly reduces the volume and complexity of the checks required to establish the structure.

The relevance of this to our situation is that the bicategory of coloured symmetric sequences
\mathsf{Sym}
can be represented as the horizontal bicategory
of a double category
\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}
in which vertical 1-cells are functions between sets. In fact, building on
[
CS10
,
FGHW18
]
, this

\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}
can be seen as a full sub-double category (on the discrete objects) of the double
category
\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}
of
categorical symmetric sequences
; which can, in turn, be constructed as
the Kleisli double category of a double monad on the double category
\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}
of profunctors.
The double monad in question maps a category
X
to its symmetric strict monoidal completion
SX
, extending the corresponding
2
-monad on the
2
-category of categories.

Given the above, the desired normal oplax monoidal structure on the bicategory of coloured symmetric sequences can be obtained as follows. Firstly
(
4.11
), we extend the results of
[
GG09
,
Shu10
,
HS19
]
to establish that such a structure can be obtained from a normal oplax monoidal structure on
\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}
, or more generally,
\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}
.
Secondly, to obtain this, we prove and apply a result (
9.4
) which isolates sufficient conditions on a double monad
T
on
a double category
\mathbb{C}
under which a monoidal structure on
\mathbb{C}
will extend to an oplax monoidal structure on the Kleisli double category
{\mathbb{K}\mathsf{l}}(T)
. Pleasingly, this condition on
T
turns out to be a natural one, namely a suitably adapted form of the
pseudo-commutativity
of
[
HP02
]
. This is satisfied by the 2-monad
S
used in our application, and indeed, the operation (
5
) featured in the definition of the arithmetic product is part of this pseudo-commutative structure on
S\colon\mathsf{Cat}\to\mathsf{Cat}
.

Thus, using this result, the monoidal structure on
\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}
given by the cartesian product of sets extends to give the arithmetic product oplax
monoidal
structure on the double category
\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}
of categorical symmetric sequences, which in turn induces the desired
oplax monoidal structure on the double category
\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}
of coloured symmetric sequences. This general method
leads exactly to the
formula in (
4
), which is a natural generalisation of that in (
1
).

While our approach offers a clear pathway to prove our main results, and others besides, we still have to overcome significant technical challenges, dealing with coherence conditions at the double categorical level, keeping track of strictness and weakness of the structures involved. Roughly speaking, vertical structure tends to be stricter than horizontal one, but the two are closely related under the assumption that the double categories under consideration are fibrant, in the sense of
[
Shu08
]
. This allows us to induce a lot of the horizontal, weaker, structure that we need for applications from vertical, stricter, one, that is already known, thereby keeping some control of the complexity of our calculations.

While it undoubtedly requires more groundwork to set up the abstract approach that we take, the end result is a modular framework which is easily
applicable to other, related situations. For example, although we shall not do so here, it is entirely straightforward to adapt our results from the
setting appropriate for studying symmetric coloured operads to the setting appropriate for many-sorted algebraic theories: it is simply a matter of
replacing the double monad
S
for symmetric strict monoidal categories with a corresponding double monad
F
for categories with strictly
associative finite products, and verifying that everything still carries through. In this setting, we obtain an oplax monoidal structure on the
appropriate Kleisli bicategory—which is essentially the bicategory of sifted-cocontinuous functors between presheaf categories—which extends the
duoidal structure on the functor category
[F(1)^{\mathrm{op}},\mathsf{Set}]
used in
[
GL16
]
to study the commuting tensor product of
single-sorted algebraic theories.

For expository convenience, we outlined our results above for
\mathsf{Set}
-valued coloured symmetric sequences, but in fact our development will be carried out in a more general enriched context. For any symmetric monoidal closed cocomplete
\mathcal{V}
there is an analogue of the
2
-monad
S
leading to a bicategory of
\mathcal{V}
-enriched symmetric sequences. However, to obtain an oplax monoidal structure on this bicategory, we will restrict to the case where the tensor product of
\mathcal{V}
is in fact
cartesian
product. The reason for this restriction, which was also made in
[
DH14
,
GL16
]
, is
that the
2
-monad
S
is only pseudo-commutative when
\mathcal{V}
is cartesian, since the structure maps in (
5
) for this pseudo-commutativity involve a ‘duplication’ of objects that is not available in
the general symmetric monoidal closed setting.

Outline of the paper

Sections

2
and
3
recall the notions of double category, double functor, horizontal and vertical transformation, and
modification. We pay particular attention to companions, leading to the notion of a special vertical transformation, and establish a few useful lemmas
about them.
Sections

4
and
5
focus on monoidal double categories, monoidal double functors, monoidal horizontal and vertical
transformations and monoidal modifications. In particular, we show that, for monoidal double categories
\mathbb{C}
and
\mathbb{D}
,
monoidal double functors between them are the objects of a functor double category (
5.6
).

Section

6
considers monoids in monoidal double categories. We use this notion in
Sections

7
and
8
to define double monads and monoidal double monads and obtain results on them in a homogeneous manner. To do this, we show that the double category of monoidal double endofunctors
on a monoidal double category admits a monoidal structure, given by composition (
8.1
).
In
Section

9
, we consider Kleisli double categories and establish sufficient conditions for a double monad on a monoidal double
category to determine a monoidal structure on the Kleisli double category. We apply these results to coloured symmetric sequences in
Section

10
, leading up to our main results on the existence of oplax monoidal structures on the relevant double category
(
10.9
) and bicategory (
10.10
).

2.
Double categories

By
double category
, we will mean a (horizontally) weak double category, also known as a pseudo double category; relevant material can be found in
[
GP99
,
GP04
,
Gar06a
,
HS19
]
.

Definition 2.1

(Double category)
.

A
double category

\mathbb{C}
consists of the following data:

•

a category
\mathbb{C}_{0}
, whose objects are
0
-cells
, and whose arrows are
vertical 1-cells

f\colon X\to X^{\prime}
;

•

a category
\mathbb{C}_{1}
, whose objects are
horizontal 1-cells

M\colon X\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow Y
, and whose arrows are
2-morphisms

(6)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y^{\prime}\mathrlap{;}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\phi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M^{\prime}}

•

two functors
\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t}\colon\mathbb{C}_{1}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{0}
called
source
and
target
respectively;

•

composition
and
identity
functors
\circ\colon\mathbb{C}_{1}\times_{\mathbb{C}_{0}}\mathbb{C}_{1}\to\mathbb{C}_{1}
and

\mathrm{id}\colon\mathbb{C}_{0}\to\mathbb{C}_{1}
;

•

natural families of globular isomorphisms in
\mathbb{C}_{1}
:

(7)

a_{M,N,P}\colon(M\circ N)\circ P\Rightarrow M\circ(N\circ P)\,,\quad\ell_{M}\colon\mathrm{id}_{Y}\circ M\Rightarrow M\quad\text{and}\quad r_{M}\colon M\circ\mathrm{id}_{X}\Rightarrow M\mathrlap{.}

These data are required to satisfy
coherence axioms analogous to those for a bicategory; see
[
GP99
, §7.1]
.

In the last item of the preceding definition, we use the notion of a
globular
2-morphism in a double category
\mathbb{C}
; this is a
2-morphism
\phi

for which
\mathbf{s}(\phi)
and

are identities:

Remark 2.2
.

In our definition of double category, vertical
1
-cells compose categorically, i.e., strictly associatively, while horizontal
1
-cells compose bicategorically, i.e., with associativity only up to coherent isomorphism. Compared to the original definition in
[
GP99
,
GP04
]
, we have chosen to interchange the vertical and horizontal directions so as to match up with later work such as
[
Gar06a
,
HS19
]
. The reader should bear this reversal of sense in mind when comparing the definitions and constructions that follow with those of
[
GP99
,
GP04
]
.

Given a double category
\mathbb{C}
, we write
\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{C})
for the its
horizontal
bicategory
, comprising the 0-cells, horizontal 1-cells and globular 2-morphisms; and we write
\mathsf{V}(\mathbb{C})
for
its
vertical 2-category
, whose objects and morphisms are the 0-cells and vertical 1-cells of
\mathbb{C}
, and where a
2
-cell
f\Rightarrow g
is a 2-morphism in
\mathbb{C}
of
the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X^{\prime}\mathrlap{.}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\phi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}_{X}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}_{X^{\prime}}}

Notice that vertical composition of 2-cells in
\mathsf{V}(\mathbb{C})
is given by pasting in the horizontal direction in
\mathbb{C}
, and vice versa.

Example 2.3

(Bicategories and monoidal categories as double
categories)
.

Any bicategory can be seen as a double
category with only identity vertical arrows. In particular, any
monoidal category
(\mathcal{V},\circ,J)
can be regarded as a double
category with a single object and only the identity vertical arrow.

Example 2.4

(The double category of matrices)
.

Fix a monoidal category
(\mathcal{V},\circ,J)
with small coproducts, such that the tensor product
preserves coproducts in each variable; in particular, this holds whenever the monoidal structure is closed. Given sets

X
and
Y
, an
(X,Y)
-
matrix

M\colon X\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow Y
is a family of objects
\bigl(M(y,x)\in\mathcal{V}:x\in X,y\in Y\bigr)
.
The double category of
\mathcal{V}
-matrices

\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
has objects and vertical
1
-cells being sets and functions, respectively;
horizontal 1-cells
M\colon X\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow Y

being
(X,Y)
-matrices; and 2-morphisms
\phi\colon M\Rightarrow N
as in (
6
) being families of
\mathcal{V}
-arrows
\bigl(\phi_{yx}\colon M(y,x)\to N(gy,fx):x\in X,y\in Y\bigr)
. Horizontal composition
N\circ M\colon X\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow Y\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow Z
is given
by

(N\circ M)(z,x)=\sum_{y\in Y}N(z,y)\circ M(y,x)\mathrlap{,}

while the horizontal identities
\mathrm{id}_{X}\colon X\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow X
are defined by
\mathrm{id}_{X}(x,x^{\prime})=J
if

x=x^{\prime}
and
\mathrm{id}_{X}(x,x^{\prime})=0
if
x\neq x^{\prime}
. The horizontal bicategory of this double category is the usual bicategory of enriched matrices; see
[
BCSW83
]
.

The choice of a different notation for
2.5
below is needed in view of
4.6
.

Example 2.5

(The double category of profunctors)
.

Fix a braided monoidal cocomplete category
(\mathcal{V},\otimes,I)
in which
the tensor product preserves colimits in each variable. Below, we use freely the standard notions of
\mathcal{V}
-category,
\mathcal{V}
-functor and

\mathcal{V}
-natural transformation, for which we invite readers to refer to
[
Kel82
]
.
Recall that, for small
\mathcal{V}
-categories
X
and
Y
, a
(Y,X)
-
profunctor

M\colon X\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow Y
is a
\mathcal{V}
-functor
M\colon Y^{\mathrm{op}}\otimes X\to\mathcal{V}
. We may now define the double category
\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
of
\mathcal{V}
-profunctors
as follows. The objects and vertical
1
-cells of
\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
are
small
\mathcal{V}
-categories and
\mathcal{V}
-functors; the horizontal

1
-cells are
\mathcal{V}
-profunctors, and squares as in (
6
) (writing now
F
and
G
instead of
f
and
g
)
are
\mathcal{V}
-natural transformations
\phi\colon M\Rightarrow M^{\prime}\,(G\otimes F)
, where

Y^{\mathrm{op}}\otimes X\xrightarrow{G\otimes F}{Y^{\prime}}^{\mathrm{op}}\otimes X^{\prime}\xrightarrow{M^{\prime}}\mathcal{V}\mathrlap{.}

Horizontal composition of
M\colon X\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow Y
and
N\colon Y\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow Z
is
given by the coend

(8)

(N\circ M)(z,x)=\int^{y\in Y}N(z,y)\otimes M(y,x)\mathrlap{.}

The horizontal identity
\mathrm{id}_{X}\colon X\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow X
is defined by
\mathrm{id}_{X}(x^{\prime},x)=X[x^{\prime},x]

2

We use brackets for hom-objects
of categories, and parentheses for applications of (pro)functors and other maps.
. Note that
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
can be regarded as
a sub-double category of
\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
by considering sets as discrete
\mathcal{V}
-categories.
The horizontal bicategory of
\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
is the familiar bicategory of profunctors, while the vertical 2-category is the 2-category
of small
\mathcal{V}
-categories.

These examples illustrate the fact, pointed out in Remark
2.2
, that in our double categorical structures, the vertical structure is strict, and relatively straightforward, while the horizontal structure is weaker and requires careful consideration of coherence issues. The management of these coherence issues is simplified when the horizontal and vertical structures can be universally related in the following way.

Although companions are defined algebraically, they also
have a universal characterisation.

Lemma 2.7
.

Let
f\colon X\rightarrow X^{\prime}
be vertical
1
-cell of a double category
\mathbb{C}
.
Giving a companion
(\widehat{f},p_{1},p_{2})
for
f
is equivalent to giving either of the following:

•

A horizontal
1
-cell
\widehat{f}
and
2
-morphism
p_{1}
as in (
9
) such that, for every horizontal
1
-cell
{M\colon X^{\prime}\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow Y^{\prime}}
, the composite
2
-morphism to the left below is cartesian with respect to
(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t})\colon\mathbb{C}_{1}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{0}\times\mathbb{C}_{0}
; or

•

A horizontal
1
-cell
\widehat{f}
and
2
-morphism
p_{2}
as in (
9
) such that, for every horizontal
1
-cell
{M\colon W\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow X}
, the composite
2
-morphism to the right below is opcartesian with respect to
(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t})\colon\mathbb{C}_{1}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{0}\times\mathbb{C}_{0}
:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow p_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}_{X^{\prime}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow r}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X^{\prime}\mathrlap{.}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\ell^{\textrm{-}1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}_{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow p_{2}}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{f}}

By virtue of this result, companions of a vertical 1-cell are
unique up to a unique globular
2
-isomorphism, so that by the usual abuse of notation we may refer simply to

the
companion. In what follows we will often
require the existence of certain companions, but in many examples
of interest we have all companions and also all
conjoints
—the
dual notion to companion, which associates to a vertical
1
-cell
f\colon X\rightarrow X^{\prime}
a horizontal
1
-cell
\widecheck{f}\colon X^{\prime}\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow X
along with unit and counit
2
-morphisms. In this case, we
may speak of a

framed bicategory
in the sense of
[
Shu08
]
or
fibrant double category
in other references. By the
above lemma and an appropriate dual lemma for conjoints, a double category is a framed bicategory if and only if
(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t})\colon\mathbb{C}_{1}\to\mathbb{C}_{0}\times\mathbb{C}_{0}
is a Grothendieck
fibration, or equivalently, a Grothendieck opfibration.

Example 2.8
.

The double category
\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
of
\mathcal{V}
-profunctors is a fibrant double category. The
companion and conjoint of a
\mathcal{V}
-functor

F\colon X\to X^{\prime}
are the
\mathcal{V}
-profunctors
\widehat{F}\colon X\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow X^{\prime}

and

\widecheck{F}\colon X^{\prime}\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow X
given by

(11)

\widehat{F}(x^{\prime},x)=X^{\prime}[x^{\prime},Fx]\quad\textrm{and}\quad\widecheck{F}(x,x^{\prime})=X^{\prime}[Fx,x^{\prime}]\mathrlap{.}

It follows
a fortiori
that the double category
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
of
matrices is also fibrant, where for a function
f\colon X\to X^{\prime}
its companion and conjoint
\widehat{f}\colon X\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow X^{\prime}
and
\widecheck{f}\colon X^{\prime}\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow X
are the
\mathcal{V}
-matrices
given by:

\widehat{f}(x^{\prime},x)=\widecheck{f}(x,x^{\prime})=\begin{cases}I&\mathrm{if}\;f(x)=x^{\prime}\mathrlap{,}\\
0&\mathrm{otherwise.}\end{cases}

Note that, in these examples, we have that
\widehat{F}\dashv\widecheck{F}
and
\widehat{f}\dashv\widecheck{f}
in the horizontal bicategory. In fact, it is
always
true that the companion and conjoint of a vertical
1
-cell are adjoint in this way.

The universality of companions in Lemma
2.7
immediately implies the following omnibus proposition.

Proposition 2.9
.

Let
\mathbb{C}
be a double category.

(1)

The vertical identity
1
-cell
1_{X}\colon X\rightarrow X
has the horizontal identity
\mathrm{id}_{X}\colon X\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow X
as a companion.

(2)

If the vertical
1
-cells
f\colon X\rightarrow X^{\prime}
and
g\colon X^{\prime}\rightarrow X^{\prime\prime}
have the companions
\widehat{f}
and
\widehat{g}
, then
g\circ f
has the companion
\widehat{g}\circ\widehat{f}
.

(3)

If the vertical
1
-cells
f\colon X\rightarrow X^{\prime}
and
g\colon Y\rightarrow Y^{\prime}
admit companions, then pasting with the companion
2
-morphisms for
f
and
g
gives a bijection between
2
-morphisms
\phi
as in
Eq.

6
and globular
2
-morphisms

(12)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{Y^{\prime}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{X^{\prime}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{Y^{\prime}}\mathrlap{.}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\widehat{\phi}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{g}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M^{\prime}}

If
f
and
g
are invertible in
\mathbb{C}_{0}
, then under this correspondence
\phi
is invertible in
\mathbb{C}_{1}
if and only if
\widehat{\phi}
is.

(4)

If
\mathsf{V}(\mathbb{C})^{\prime}
denotes the locally full sub-
2
-category of
\mathsf{V}(\mathbb{C})
with the same objects, and as
morphisms just those the vertical
1
-cells which admit companions, then taking companions underlies an identity-on-objects homomorphism of
bicategories
\mathsf{V}(\mathbb{C})^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{C})
.

(5)

If
f\colon X\rightarrow X^{\prime}
is a vertical
1
-isomorphism in
\mathbb{C}
and both
f
and
f^{\textrm{-}1}
admit companions, then
\smash{\widehat{f}}
is an
equivalence in
\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{C})
with pseudoinverse
\smash{\widehat{f^{\textrm{-}1}}}
;

(6)

If
\phi\colon f\Rightarrow g
is an invertible
2
-cell in
\mathsf{V}(\mathbb{C})
, and
f
and
g
admit companions, then
\widehat{\phi}
is an invertible globular
2
-morphism
\widehat{f}\Rightarrow\widehat{g}
in
\mathbb{C}
.

3.
Maps of double categories

In this section, we recall the various kinds of maps existing between double categories, starting with the notions of double functor and oplax double functor. In most of the paper we will work with double functors, which
preserve composition and identities up to isomorphism. However, we will also need oplax double functors, which preserve composition and identities only up to a non-invertible 2-cell, in one important situation, namely when we define
oplax monoidal structure in
4.1
.

Definition 3.1

(Oplax double functor, double functor)
.

Let
\mathbb{C}
and
\mathbb{D}
be double categories. An
oplax double functor

F\colon\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{D}

consists of the following data:

•

two ordinary functors
F_{0}\colon\mathbb{C}_{0}\to\mathbb{D}_{0}
,

F_{1}\colon\mathbb{C}_{1}\to\mathbb{D}_{1}
, denoted by the same letter
F
below, such that
\mathbf{s}F_{1}=F_{0}\mathbf{s}
and
\mathbf{t}F_{1}=F_{0}\mathbf{t}
, as displayed in:

{}{}}}{
{}{}}
{{}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{}{{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
}{{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{-44.46521pt}{-19.83531pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform} \pgfsys@hbox{60}\lxSVG@closescope }}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}}}{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}}}
\lxSVG@closescope }}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\xi_{X}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}_{FX}}

These data are required to satisfy coherence conditions similar to those for an oplax functor between bicategories,
one regarding associativity and two for unitality; see
[
GP99
, §7.2]
.

A
(pseudo) double functor

F\colon\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{D}
is an oplax double
functor for which the 2-cells
\xi_{M,N}
and
\xi_{X}
are invertible.

Lemma 3.2
.

Let
F\colon\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{D}
be an oplax (pseudo) double functor. Then
F
induces an oplax (pseudo) functor of bicategories
\mathcal{H}(F)\colon\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{C})\to\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D})
.
This assignment extends to an ordinary functor from the category of double categories and oplax (pseudo) double functors to the
category of bicategories and oplax (pseudo) functors.

Proof.

This follows from the definition, and is an oplax analogue of
[
HS19
, Theorem 4.1]
.
Recall that functors of double categories and bicategories compose strictly associatively.
∎

Lemma 3.3
.

Let
F\colon\mathbb{C}\rightarrow\mathbb{D}
be a double functor and
f\colon X\rightarrow X^{\prime}
a
vertical
1
-cell of
\mathbb{C}
. Assume that
f
admits a companion
\widehat{f}
with structure cells
p_{1},p_{2}
. Then the vertical
1
-cell

of
\mathbb{D}
admits the companion

via the structure cells

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces FX}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces FX^{\prime}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces FX^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces FX^{\prime}\mathrlap{.}}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Ff}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\xi_{X^{\prime}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}_{FX^{\prime}}}

and

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces FX}

In future, we will tend to suppress the unit coherence cells
\xi
appearing above, and simply write
Fp_{1}
and
Fp_{2}
for these pasting composites.

Since a double category has two kinds of
1
-cell, vertical and horizontal, there are
two kinds of natural transformations between double functors,
vertical and horizontal, depending on the directions of their components.
For our applications, it is the
horizontal
transformations, recalled in
3.4
, which will be most important, since these induce structure on the horizontal bicategory. However, the
vertical
transformations, recalled in
3.5
, are simpler to construct and work with, and so fundamental to our development will be the possibility of turning a vertical natural transformation into a horizontal
one in the presence of well-behaved companions. The precise conditions needed are isolated in the
the notion of a special vertical transformation (
3.6
), and are justified in
3.10
, where we show that the special vertical transformations are exactly the vertical
1
-cells of the functor double category (
3.9
) which admit companions.

The following definition can be found, for example, in
[
Gar06b
, §2.4]
; or in
[
GP99
, §7.4]
under the name ‘strong vertical transformation’ (recalling the reversal of sense of Remark
2.2
).

Definition 3.5

(Vertical transformation)
.

\mathbb{D}

between double functors induces a pseudonatural transformation
\mathcal{H}(\beta)\colon\mathcal{H}(F)\Rightarrow\mathcal{H}(F^{\prime})
between the associated homomorphisms of bicategories. On the other hand, from a vertical transformation
\sigma\colon F\Rightarrow F^{\prime}
, there is no direct way of inducing anything
\mathcal{H}(F)\Rightarrow\mathcal{H}(F^{\prime})
. However, there is an indirect way of doing so, if we can first turn the vertical transformation

\sigma\colon F\Rightarrow F^{\prime}

Definition 3.6

(Special vertical transformation)
.

Let
\sigma\colon F\Rightarrow F^{\prime}
be a vertical transformation between oplax double functors
\mathbb{C}\rightarrow\mathbb{D}
. We say that
\sigma
is

special
if for every
X\in\mathbb{C}
, the vertical
1
-cell component
\sigma_{X}\colon FX\rightarrow F^{\prime}X

has a companion
\widehat{\sigma}_{X}\colon FX\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow F^{\prime}X
in
\mathbb{D}
, and the
companion transposes

(20)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces FX}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces FY}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F^{\prime}Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces FX}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F^{\prime}X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F^{\prime}Y}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces FM}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\widehat{\sigma}_{M}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{\sigma}_{Y}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{\sigma}_{X}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F^{\prime}M}

of the
2
-morphism components (
16
) of
\sigma
are invertible.

loosely strong companions
in

∎

Proposition 3.9

(Functor double categories)
.

Let
\mathbb{C}
and
\mathbb{D}
be double categories.
There is a double category
\mathsf{DblCat}[\mathbb{C},\mathbb{D}]
(resp.,
\mathsf{DblCat}_{\mathrm{oplax}}[\mathbb{C},\mathbb{D}]
) composed of double functors from
\mathbb{C}
to
\mathbb{D}
(resp., oplax double functors), vertical transformations, horizontal
transformations and modifications.

4.
Monoidal double categories

The aim of this section is to introduce the notions of
monoidal double category
and
oplax monoidal double category
, and to
prove some useful facts about them. Both notions describe double categories endowed with a monoidal product: the key difference is that in the former
case, this tensor product is a double functor, while in the latter case, it is merely an oplax double functor as in
3.1
. In
particular, it should be emphasised that ‘oplax’ only modifies the functoriality of
the tensor product, rather than the nature of the associativity and unit constraints for this tensor, which for us will always be invertible.

In what follows, we will be concerned with the the question of extending a
monoidal
structure on a double category to an
oplax monoidal

structure on an associated Kleisli double category. Since we need both notions, we here define them simultaneously.

Definition 4.1

(Oplax monoidal double category, monoidal double category)
.

Let
\mathbb{C}
be a double category. An
oplax monoidal structure
on
\mathbb{C}
consists of the following data:

•

an oplax double functor
\otimes\colon\mathbb{C}\times\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}
;

•

an oplax double functor
I\colon\mathbf{1}\to\mathbb{C}
;

•

invertible vertical transformations
\alpha\colon\mathord{\otimes}\circ(1\times\mathord{\otimes})\Rightarrow\mathord{\otimes}\circ(\mathord{\otimes}\times 1)
,

\lambda\colon\mathord{\otimes}\circ(I\times 1)\Rightarrow 1
and
\rho\colon\mathord{\otimes}\circ(1\times I)\Rightarrow 1

satisfying the usual Mac Lane coherence axioms for
\alpha
,
\lambda
and
\rho
.
Said another way, this structure amounts to the following:

•

monoidal structures
(\otimes_{0},I_{0})
and
(\otimes_{1},I_{1})
on the categories
\mathbb{C}_{0}
and
\mathbb{C}_{1}
;

•

strict
monoidality of
\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t}\colon\mathbb{C}_{1}\rightrightarrows\mathbb{C}_{0}
. For example, the associativity
constraint for
\mathbb{C}_{1}
has components

(22)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(X_{1}\otimes X_{2})\otimes X_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(Y_{1}\otimes Y_{2})\otimes Y_{3}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{1}\otimes(X_{2}\otimes X_{3})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y_{1}\otimes(Y_{2}\otimes Y_{3})\mathrlap{;}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(M_{1}\otimes M_{2})\otimes M_{3}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{X_{1},X_{2},X_{3}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\alpha_{M_{1},M_{2},M_{3}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha_{Y_{1},Y_{2},Y_{3}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M_{1}\otimes(M_{2}\otimes M_{3})}

•

globular 2-morphisms

(23)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{1}\otimes X_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z_{1}\otimes Z_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{1}\otimes X_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y_{1}\otimes Y_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z_{1}\otimes Z_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(N_{1}\circ M_{1})\otimes(N_{2}\circ M_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\tau}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M_{1}\otimes M_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces N_{1}\otimes N_{2}}

and

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{1}\otimes X_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{1}\otimes X_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{1}\otimes X_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{1}\otimes X_{2}\mathrlap{,}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}_{X_{1}}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{X_{2}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\eta}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}_{X_{1}\otimes X_{2}}}

subject to axioms that make
\otimes
into an oplax double functor;

•

globular 2-morphisms

(24)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\delta}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I_{1}}

and

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I_{0}\mathrlap{,}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\iota}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}_{I_{0}}}

subject to axioms that make
I
into an oplax double functor;

•

two axioms ensuring that the associativity constraint
\alpha
is a vertical
transformation between oplax double functors;

•

four axioms ensuring that the unit constraints
\lambda
and
\rho
are vertical
transformations between oplax double functors.

The above axioms are written explicitly in
Section

A.1
.
We have a
monoidal double category
when the tensor and unit are specified by double functors, rather than oplax double
functors; said another way, when each of the
2
-morphisms in (
23
) and (
24
) is invertible.

What we call here an oplax monoidal double category is what is called simply a monoidal double category in

[
GP04
, §5.5]
; it is equally well a pseudomonoid in the cartesian monoidal 2-category of double categories, oplax double
functors and vertical transformations.

Remark 4.2
.

We defined a monoidal double category to be an oplax monoidal double category
satisfying some additional properties; but these additional properties in fact allow us to simplify the structure further, as explained
in
[
HS19
, Page 8]
. Indeed, in a monoidal double category, the monoidal unit

I_{1}
of
\mathbb{C}_{1}
is always canonically isomorphic to
\mathrm{id}_{I_{0}}
via
\iota
; and it does no harm to assume that, in fact,
I_{1}
is
\mathrm{id}_{I_{0}}

and
\iota
is the identity
2
-morphism—which in turn forces
\delta=\ell_{\mathrm{id}_{I_{0}}}=r_{\mathrm{id}_{I_{0}}}
for the
globular isomorphisms (
7
) for horizontal identities in
\mathbb{C}
.
As such, if in specifying a monoidal double category we follow these conventions, then we need only provide the invertible
structure 2-morphisms
\tau
and
\eta
satisfying the appropriate coherence axioms.
By contrast, in an oplax monoidal double category, none of the data are redundant: indeed,
\delta
and
\iota
as in
Eq.

24
now
specify a
comonad
structure on
I_{1}
in
\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{C})
, see
Eq.

80
.

Moreover, notice that just as a double category is an internal pseudocategory in
the 2-category of small categories, functors and natural transformations,
an oplax monoidal double category is an internal pseudocategory in the
2
-category of monoidal categories,
lax monoidal functors and monoidal transformations for which the
source and target functors are strict monoidal.

As mentioned in the introduction, the notion of oplax monoidal structure will be exploited in future work in order to provide a general notion of
commuting tensor product
, generalising the theory of
[
GL16
]
, which will in particular recover the Boardman–Vogt tensor product of symmetric coloured operads and its extension to operadic bimodules in
[
DH14
]
. For these applications, it will be important that the oplax monoidal structure is
normal
in the sense of the following definition.

Definition 4.3

(Normal oplax monoidal double category)
.

An oplax monoidal double category
\mathbb{C}
is said to be
normal
if:

(1)

I\colon\mathbf{1}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}
is a (pseudo) double functor;

(2)

for all objects
X_{1},X_{2}\in\mathbb{C}
, the following restricted oplax double functors are (pseudo) double functors:

(25)

X_{1}\otimes({\mathord{\text{--}}})\colon\mathbb{C}\cong\mathbf{1}\times\mathbb{C}\xrightarrow{X_{1}\times\mathbb{C}}\mathbb{C}\times\mathbb{C}\xrightarrow{\otimes}\mathbb{C}\ \ \text{and}\ \ ({\mathord{\text{--}}})\otimes X_{2}\colon\mathbb{C}\cong\mathbb{C}\times\mathbf{1}\xrightarrow{\mathbb{C}\times X_{2}}\mathbb{C}\times\mathbb{C}\xrightarrow{\otimes}\mathbb{C}\mathrlap{.}

Said another way, both
2
-morphisms
\delta
and
\iota
in (
24
) are invertible; while in (
23
),
\eta

is invertible, and each
\tau
for which
M_{1}=N_{1}=\mathrm{id}_{X_{1}}
or
M_{2}=N_{2}=\mathrm{id}_{X_{2}}
is also invertible.

We give now some examples of monoidal double categories and oplax monoidal double categories. The example of profunctors in
4.7
will be
fundamental for our application in
Section

10
.

Example 4.4

(Duoidal categories)
.

Recall from
2.3
that a monoidal category
(\mathcal{V},\circ,J)
is the same thing as a double category with
a single object and only identity vertical arrow. To equip this double category
with an oplax monoidal structure in the sense of
4.1

is the same thing as equipping
\mathcal{V}
with additional structure making it into a duoidal category
[
AM10
]
.
Explicitly, this amounts to providing a second monoidal structure
(\otimes,I)
on
\mathcal{V}
, along with maps

\displaystyle\xi\colon(Y_{1}\circ X_{1})\otimes(Y_{2}\circ X_{2})\to(Y_{1}\otimes Y_{2})\circ(X_{1}\otimes X_{2})\text{,}

\displaystyle\mu\colon J\otimes J\to J\text{,}\qquad\gamma\colon I\to I\circ I\text{,}\qquad\nu\colon I\to J\mathrlap{,}

satisfying appropriate axioms. Here, the interchange law
\xi
corresponds to the square
\tau
in
Eq.

23
.

This oplax monoidal structure is a genuine monoidal structure whenever all of
\xi
,
\mu
,
\gamma
and
\nu
are invertible. In this case, by the
Eckmann–Hilton argument, the identity functor underlies a monoidal isomorphism
(\mathcal{V},\otimes,I)\rightarrow(\mathcal{V},\circ,J)
, and the two
isomorphic monoidal structures are each
braided
. Loosely, then, we may say that in this situation,
\mathcal{V}
‘is’ a braided monoidal
category. In particular, if we merely start with a braided monoidal category
(\mathcal{V},\otimes,I)
, then it becomes duoidal on taking
\mathord{\circ}=\mathord{\otimes}
,
J=I
,
\nu=\mathrm{id}
,
\mu=r_{I}
,
\gamma=r_{I}^{\textrm{-}1}
, and
\xi
the canonical constraint built from associativity and braiding
maps.

Returning to the general situation, the oplax monoidal structure on
\mathcal{V}

qua
double category is normal if, and only if, the duoidal
structure on
\mathcal{V}
is
normal
meaning that
\nu
,
\gamma
and
\mu
are all invertible. Indeed, to say that the unit double functor of the oplax monoidal structure is pseudo is precisely to say that
\gamma
and
\nu
are invertible, which by the duoidal axioms implies the invertibility of
\mu
also. So the duoidal structure on
\mathcal{V}
is normal precisely when its oplax monoidal structure
qua
double category satisfies
4.3
1
. What is less obvious is that, in this one-object case,
4.3
2
is an automatic consequence of
4.3
1
; but
2
in this case amounts to the invertibility of
\xi
when
X_{1}=Y_{1}=J
or
X_{2}=Y_{2}=J
, and this follow from the oplax monoidality of the unit constraints for
\otimes
.

Remark 4.5
.

Looking at the previous example, the reader may wonder why we impose
4.3
2
at all, given that
4.3
1
by itself gives a faithful “many-object” generalisation of the notion of normal duoidal category. The reason for imposing the extra condition is that it ensures companions in our double category are stable under tensoring by objects, which will be crucial when we come to show that normal oplax monoidal double categories give rise to normal oplax monoidal bicategories—see the proofs of
4.10
and
4.11
below. A second justification for the condition comes from work-in-progress, which generalises the theory of commuting tensor products developed
in
[
GL16
]
to a “many-object” setting. In this generalisation, the normal duoidal categories used as an enrichment base in
op. cit.
will be replaced with normal oplax monoidal double categories in the above sense—and, again,
4.3
2
will be necessary in order to make any progress with the theory.

Example 4.6

(Oplax monoidal structure on
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
)
.

Recall from
2.4
that, for a monoidal category
(\mathcal{V},\circ,J)

in which the tensor product preserves coproducts in each variable,
we have a double category
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
of
\mathcal{V}
-matrices. If
\mathcal{V}
is further
equipped with a second monoidal structure
(\otimes,I)
which also preserves coproducts in each variable, and data
as above making it into a duoidal category, then
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
acquires an
oplax monoidal structure.
The tensor product is given by the cartesian product of
sets and functions on the vertical level, and for
\mathcal{V}
-matrices
M_{1}\colon X_{1}\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow Y_{1}
and
M_{2}\colon X_{2}\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow Y_{2}
the tensor
M_{1}\otimes M_{2}\colon X_{1}\times X_{2}\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow Y_{1}\times Y_{2}
defined by letting

(M_{1}\otimes M_{2})((y_{1},y_{2}),(x_{1},x_{2}))=M_{1}(y_{1},x_{1})\otimes M_{2}(y_{2},x_{2})\mathrlap{.}

The monoidal unit is
I\colon 1\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow 1
with unique component

I_{*,*}=I
. The structure cells
Eq.

23
and
Eq.

24
are formed
using the duoidal structure maps, with the most complex case being that the
2
-morphism
\tau\colon(N_{1}\circ M_{1})\otimes(N_{2}\circ M_{2})\to(N_{1}\otimes N_{2})\circ(M_{1}\otimes M_{2})
has components:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\big(\sum_{y_{1}}N_{1}(z_{1},y_{1})\circ M_{1}(y_{1},x_{1})\big)\otimes\bigl(\sum_{y_{2}}N_{2}(z_{2},y_{2})\circ M_{2}(y_{2},x_{2})\bigr)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sum_{y_{1},y_{2}}\big(N_{1}(z_{1},y_{1})\circ M_{1}(y_{1},x_{1})\big)\otimes\bigl(N_{2}(z_{2},y_{2})\circ M_{2}(y_{2},x_{2})\bigr)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sum_{y_{1},y_{2}}\bigl(N_{1}(z_{1},y_{1})\otimes N_{2}(z_{2},y_{2})\bigr)\circ\bigl(M_{1}(y_{1},x_{1})\otimes M_{2}(y_{2},x_{2})\bigr)\mathrlap{.}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cong}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sum_{y_{1},y_{2}}\xi}

It is not hard to see that this oplax monoidal structure is normal precisely when
\mathcal{V}
is normal as a duoidal category in the sense of the
preceding example, and that it is genuinely monoidal just when the duoidal structure of
\mathcal{V}
comes from a braided monoidal structure.

Example 4.7

(Monoidal structure on
\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
)
.

Let
\mathcal{V}
be a braided monoidal category in
which the tensor product preserves colimits in each variable and recall the
double category
\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
of
2.5
.
This double category admits a monoidal structure extending that of
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
in the braided case.
On objects and vertical
1
-cells, this is simply the monoidal structure of the 2-category
\mathsf{Cat}_{\mathcal{V}}
.
On horizontal
1
-cells, given
\mathcal{V}
-profunctors
M_{1}\colon X_{1}\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow Y_{1}
and
M_{2}\colon X_{2}\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow Y_{2}
, the

\mathcal{V}
-profunctor
M_{1}\otimes M_{2}\colon X_{1}\otimes Y_{2}\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow Y_{1}\otimes Y_{2}
is given by

(26)

(M_{1}\otimes M_{2})\bigl((y_{1},y_{2})(x_{1},x_{2})\bigr)=M_{1}(y_{1},x_{1})\otimes M_{2}(y_{2},x_{2})\mathrlap{,}

with a corresponding definition on
2
-morphisms.
The key structure isomorphism
\tau
in
Eq.

23
is formed using the
braiding of the tensor product on
\mathcal{V}
and the fact that it preserves colimits in each variable.

One can carry out the construction above also when
\mathcal{V}
is merely a duoidal category, thereby extending
4.6
, but
we shall not need this level of generality for our application in
Section

10
.

One of the main results of
[
HS19
]
, building on
[
Shu10
,
GG09
]
, is that under suitable
assumptions, the horizontal bicategory of a monoidal double category
is a monoidal bicategory in the sense of
[
GPS95
]
; see Theorem 1.1 of
op. cit.
In view of our application in

Section

10
, we would like a generalisation of this result which endows the horizontal bicategory of an oplax monoidal double category
with an oplax monoidal structure.

The first obstacle to be faced is the definition of oplax monoidal structure on a bicategory
\mathcal{K}
. As before, ‘oplax’ refers to the strictness
of the tensor product functor, and so we might attempt the following naive adaptation of the usual notion of monoidal bicategory.
Firstly, we would require oplax functors of bicategories

\otimes\colon\mathcal{K}\times\mathcal{K}\to\mathcal{K}

and
I\colon\mathbf{1}\to\mathcal{K}
; then
pseudonatural equivalences

(27)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{K}^{3}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{K}^{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{K}^{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{K}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathord{\otimes}\times 1}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 1\times\mathord{\otimes}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\alpha}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\otimes}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\otimes}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{K}^{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{K}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{K}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\otimes}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\lambda}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I\times 1}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 1}

and

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{K}^{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{K}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{K}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\otimes}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\rho}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 1\times I}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 1}

giving the associativity and unit constraints; then invertible modifications

(28)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{K}^{3}}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\otimes}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{K}^{3}}

witnessing the pseudo-coherence of the constraint cells; and, finally, the appropriate coherence axioms for these pseudo-coherences, as found, for
example, in
[
McC99
, §A.1]
.

The problem with this definition can be seen in (
28
) above. In the domain of
\pi
we have, among other things, the pseudonatural
transformation
\alpha\times 1
whiskered by the oplax functor
\otimes\colon\mathcal{K}^{2}\rightarrow\mathcal{K}
. However, such a composition
does

not
yield another pseudonatural transformation, nor even a lax or oplax transformation. So
\pi
is not well-defined; and similar issues
arise for
\mu
,
L
and
R
in (
29
) and (
30
).

We will resolve this issue by imposing a further constraint on the components of the pseudonatural equivalences
\alpha,\lambda,\rho
of

Eq.

27
which we will term
centrality
, loosely inspired by the nomenclature of
[
PR97
]
. Centrality of the components
of a pseudonatural transformation
\gamma
will ensure that composites of the form
\gamma\otimes 1\mathrel{\mathop{:}}=\otimes\circ(\gamma\times 1)
and
1\otimes\gamma\mathrel{\mathop{:}}=\otimes\circ(1\times\gamma)
are well-defined pseudonatural transformations; and, furthermore, that the same pseudonaturality
holds for any iterated tensorings such as
((1\otimes\gamma)\otimes 1)\otimes 1
. Applied to the case of
\alpha
,
\lambda
and
\rho
, this will
ensure that the transformations appearing in
Eqs.

28
to
30
, as well as all of those appearing in the corresponding
coherence axioms, make sense.

Definition 4.8
.

Let
\mathcal{K}
be a bicategory endowed with an oplax functor
(\otimes,\tau,\eta)\colon\mathcal{K}\times\mathcal{K}\to\mathcal{K}
, an oplax functor
(I,\delta,\iota)\colon 1\rightarrow\mathcal{K}
and pseudonatural equivalences as in (
27
).
A 1-cell
f\colon X\to Y
of
\mathcal{K}
is said to be

central
when for all maps
g\colon X^{\prime}\rightarrow X
,
h\colon Y\rightarrow Y^{\prime}
,
k\colon U\rightarrow W
and
\ell\colon V\rightarrow Z
, the following composite oplax structure cells are invertible:

(31)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(U\otimes X)\otimes V}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(W\otimes Y^{\prime})\otimes Z}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(U\otimes Y)\otimes V}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces((k\otimes h)\circ(\mathrm{id}\otimes f))\otimes\ell}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(k\otimes(h\circ f))\otimes\ell}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\mathrm{id}\otimes f)\otimes\mathrm{id}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\tau}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\tau\otimes 1_{\ell}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(k\otimes h)\otimes\ell}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(U\otimes X^{\prime})\otimes V}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(W\otimes Y)\otimes Z\hbox to0.0pt{ .\hss}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(W\otimes X)\otimes Z}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces((\mathrm{id}\otimes f)\circ(k\otimes g))\otimes\ell}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(k\otimes(f\circ g))\otimes\ell}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(k\otimes g)\otimes\ell}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\tau}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\tau\otimes 1_{\ell}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\mathrm{id}\otimes f)\otimes\mathrm{id}}

Note that in (
31
), we consider three-fold tensor products bracketed to the
left
. We could equally have chosen to bracket to the
right
, but this would make no difference, since composing (
31
) with the components of
\alpha
and their pseudoinverses would yield invertibility of the corresponding cells for the other bracketing.

Now, by taking
k=\mathrm{id}_{I}
or
\ell=\mathrm{id}_{I}
in (
31
), and composing with the
components of
\lambda
or
\rho
and their pseudoinverses, we obtain the invertibility of oplax constraints of the
following forms:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X\otimes V}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y^{\prime}\otimes Z}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y\otimes V}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\tau}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(h\circ f)\otimes\ell}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f\otimes\mathrm{id}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h\otimes\ell}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X^{\prime}\otimes V}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y\otimes Z}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X\otimes Z}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\tau}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(f\circ g)\otimes\ell}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g\otimes\ell}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f\otimes\mathrm{id}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U\otimes X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W\otimes Y^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U\otimes Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\tau}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces k\otimes(h\circ f)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}\otimes f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces k\otimes h}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U\otimes X^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W\otimes Y\hbox to0.0pt{ .\hss}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W\otimes X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\tau}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces k\otimes(f\circ g)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces k\otimes g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}\otimes f}

Because of this, if
\gamma\colon F\Rightarrow G\colon\mathcal{L}\rightarrow\mathcal{K}
is a pseudonatural transformation with central components, then both
\gamma\otimes 1
and
1\otimes\gamma
will also be pseudonatural; for example, in the case of
\gamma\otimes 1
, the pseudonaturality with respect to
f\colon X\to Y
and
g\colon C\to D

is witnessed by the invertible
2
-cell

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces FX\otimes C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces FY\otimes D}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces GX\otimes C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces GY\otimes D\hbox to0.0pt{ .\hss}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Ff\otimes g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\gamma_{X}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{C}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\gamma_{Y}\circ Ff)\otimes g}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\tau^{-1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(Gf\circ\gamma_{X})\otimes g}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\scriptstyle\Downarrow\gamma_{f}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{g}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\tau}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\gamma_{Y}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{D}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Gf\otimes g}

In a similar way, the general form of (
31
) implies that
(1\otimes\gamma)\otimes 1
is also pseudonatural; note that this does

not
seem to follow from the pseudonaturality of
1\otimes\gamma
and
\gamma\otimes 1
. However, once we have pseudonaturality of
(1\otimes\gamma)\otimes 1
, we obtain
a fortiori
that of, say,
(1\otimes\gamma)\otimes(1\otimes 1)
and so by composing with the
equivalence components of
\alpha
, the pseudonaturality of
((1\otimes\gamma)\otimes 1)\otimes 1
. By following this pattern, we see that

any
tensoring of
\gamma
with identity pseudonatural transformations will again be pseudonatural.

In particular, if we require the pseudonatural transformations
\alpha
,
\lambda
and
\rho
to themselves have central components, then we see that
every
2
-cell pasting which appears in the axioms
Eqs.

28
to
30
will be a well-defined pseudonatural transformation,
and likewise for the pastings appearing in the coherence axioms. Thus, we are justified in giving:

Definition 4.9
.

Let
\mathcal{K}
be a bicategory. An
oplax monoidal structure
on
\mathcal{K}
consists of:

•

an oplax functor of bicategories
\otimes\colon\mathcal{K}\times\mathcal{K}\to\mathcal{K}
;

•

an oplax homomorphism
I\colon\mathbf{1}\to\mathcal{K}
;

•

pseudonatural equivalences
\alpha,\lambda,\rho
as in (
27
), whose components are central;

•

invertible modifications
\pi,\mu,L,R
as in (
28
)–(
30
);

satisfying the coherence axioms for a monoidal bicategory as found, for example, in
[
McC99
, §A.1]
.
Like in
4.3
, we say that the oplax monoidal structure on
\mathcal{K}
is
normal
if
I\colon 1\rightarrow\mathcal{K}
is a homomorphism of bicategories, and
\otimes
is pseudo in each variable,
i.e.
for each
X,Y\in\mathcal{K}
the oplax functors
X\otimes({\mathord{\text{--}}})\colon\mathcal{K}\rightarrow\mathcal{K}
and

({\mathord{\text{--}}})\otimes Y\colon\mathcal{K}\rightarrow\mathcal{K}
are homomorphisms of bicategories.

We now explain how a normal oplax monoidal double category
\mathbb{C}
gives rise to a normal oplax monoidal bicategory. First of all, the oplax double functor
\otimes
and the pseudo double functor
I
induce
functors on the horizontal bicategory

(32)

\otimes\colon\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{C})\times\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{C})\to\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{C}),\quad I\colon\mathbf{1}\to\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{C})

which we denote with the same symbol. Here, as per
3.2
,
\otimes
is an oplax functor of bicategories (which is pseudo in each variable) and
I
is a homomorphism of
bicategories.
If now we assume that the components of the invertible vertical transformations
\alpha
,
\lambda
and
\rho
associated to the monoidal structure on
\mathbb{C}
have companions, then they will induce
pseudonatural equivalences

(33)

\widehat{\alpha}\colon\mathord{\otimes}\circ(1\times\mathord{\otimes})\Rightarrow\mathord{\otimes}\circ(\mathord{\otimes}\times 1)\qquad\widehat{\lambda}\colon\mathord{\otimes}\circ(I\times 1)\Rightarrow 1\qquad\widehat{r}\colon 1\Rightarrow\mathord{\otimes}\circ(1\times I)

between oplax functors of bicategories, according to
3.11

and since
\mathcal{H}
is functorial. To proceed further, we need the components of
\widehat{\alpha},\widehat{\lambda}
and
\widehat{\rho}
to be central. This will be a consequence of the following lemma.
Note that
normality
of the oplax monoidal structure on
\mathbb{C}
is important
for the proof. It is not clear to us if the corresponding result without it would hold; however, since normality will be present in our applications, we have not pursued this point any further.

Theorem 4.11
.

If

5.
Maps of monoidal double categories

For our development in
Sections

7
and
8
, we will need results concerning both double monads and pseudomonoidal double monads. It turns out that many of these results can be proved uniformly across the two cases, by exhibiting both kind of structure as monoids in suitable endofunctor double categories. This is much as ordinary monads and monoidal monads can be seen as monoids in appropriate endofunctor categories.
In order to do this for the case of pseudomonoidal double monads, we need to construct a suitable double category of (lax) monoidal double functors
and monoidal transformations. While the notions of lax monoidal double functor and monoidal horizontal transformation (recalled in

5.1
and
5.2
below) are as expected, it turns out that in our motivating examples, the vertical
transformations which we need are not monoidal in the obvious way but only
pseudomonoidal
. While this
may seem an innocuous change, it adds an additional layer of subtlety to our development,
very much in analogy with what happens in the purely 2-categorical setting
[
HP02
]
.

We begin with the notion of a lax monoidal double functor. If we view monoidal double categories as pseudomonoids in a
2
-category of double categories, double functors and vertical transformations, then the lax monoidal functors are simply the lax morphisms of pseudomonoids. This definition can also be found in
[
HS19
, Definition 2.14]
, though note that there, the (invertible) structure maps
\tau
and
\eta
of a monoidal
double category (
4.1
) are oriented in the opposite direction.

Definition 5.1

(Lax monoidal double functor)
.

Let
\mathbb{C}
and
\mathbb{D}
be monoidal double categories. A
lax monoidal
double functor

F\colon\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{D}
is a (pseudo) double functor equipped with:

•

a vertical transformation
F^{2}\colon\mathord{\otimes}\circ(F\times F)\Rightarrow F\circ\mathord{\otimes}
,
whose vertical
1
-cell components we denote by
F^{2}_{X_{1},X_{2}}\colon FX_{1}\otimes FX_{2}\to F(X_{1}\otimes X_{2})
, and whose
2
-morphism components we denote by

(36)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces FX_{1}\otimes FX_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces FY_{1}\otimes FY_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(X_{1}\otimes X_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(Y_{1}\otimes Y_{2})\mathrlap{;}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces FM\otimes FN}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F^{2}_{X_{1},X_{2}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow F^{2}_{M,N}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F^{2}_{Y_{1},Y_{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(M\otimes N)}

•

a vertical transformation
F^{0}\colon I_{\mathbb{D}}\Rightarrow F\circ I_{\mathbb{C}}
,
whose vertical
1
-cell component we denote by
F^{0}\colon I\to FI
and whose
2
-morphism component we
denote by

(37)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces FI}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces FI\mathrlap{;}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}_{I}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F^{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow{}}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(\mathrm{id}_{I})}

subject to axioms expressing that the vertical
1
-cells

and

endow

with the structure of a lax monoidal functor, and that the
2
-morphisms of (
36
)
and (
37
) do the same for
F_{1}\colon\mathbb{C}_{0}\rightarrow\mathbb{D}_{0}
.

The reader will notice that we have not named the
2
-morphism in (

). This is because its definition is forced: for indeed, since
F^{0}
is a vertical transformation between double functors, the axiom
Eq.

19
causes (

) to be equal to
\mathrm{id}_{F^{0}}
followed by the unit structure isomorphism of
F
.

We now turn to monoidal transformations between lax monoidal double functors. We begin with the horizontal case, which is as expected, though we could not find it in the literature.

expressing that the natural transformation giving the globular cell
components of
\beta
is a monoidal natural transformation. (Note that the ‘nullary’ axiom corresponding to this ‘binary’ axiom holds automatically and need not be stated explicitly.)

We now consider monoidality of vertical transformations. Given the view of monoidal double categories and lax monoidal double functors as pseudomonoids and lax pseudomonoid maps, the obvious thing to consider would be the corresponding transformations of pseudomonoids, and this would yield the notion of monoidal vertical transformation considered in
[
HS19
, Definition 2.15]
. However, we will need something slightly more general for our applications (
cf.

5.4
), which we will term a
pseudomonoidal
vertical transformation. The difference can be appreciated by noting that monoidality of a vertical transformation in the sense of
loc. cit.
makes the underlying
2
-natural transformation on the vertical
2
-category into a
\mathsf{Cat}
-enriched monoidal transformation, while for our transformations, this underlying
2
-natural transformation is only a
monoidal pseudonatural transformation
in the sense of
[
DS97
, Definition 3]
.

Definition 5.3

(Pseudomonoidal vertical transformation)
.

Let
F\,,F^{\prime}\colon\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{D}
be lax monoidal double functors.
A
pseudomonoidal vertical transformation

\sigma\colon F\Rightarrow F^{\prime}

is a vertical transformation equipped with squares

Note that the final four of these axioms only involve structure in the vertical
2
-category
\mathsf{V}(\mathbb{D})
; and in fact, they correspond exactly to the axioms for a monoidal pseudonatural transformation from
[
DS97
, Definition 3]
. More explicitly, the second axiom expresses that the
2
-cells
\sigma^{2}_{X_{1},X_{2}}
are components of a modification, while the third through fifth axioms are precisely the three coherence axioms of
loc. cit.

If
\sigma^{0}
and the components of
\sigma^{2}
are identity 2-cells, then
\sigma
becomes a

monoidal
vertical transformation in the sense of

[
HS19
, Definition 2.15]
.
In that case,
\sigma_{0}\colon F_{0}\Rightarrow F^{\prime}_{0}
and
\sigma_{1}\colon F_{1}\Rightarrow F^{\prime}_{1}
are monoidal transformations in the usual sense between lax
monoidal functors.

Remark 5.4
.

The notion of a monoidal (rather than pseudomonoidal) vertical transformation
is insufficiently general for the situation we are interested in:
the monoidality of the free symmetric monoidal category double monad on the double category of
small categories, functors and profunctors, as considered in
Section

10
. The underlying double
functor of this double monad can be equipped with lax monoidal structure, with respect to which the monad unit is a
monoidal
vertical transformation; however, the monad multiplication is not a monoidal as a vertical transformation, but
only
pseudomonoidal
. This can be seen as a consequence of the fact that the free symmetric monoidal category monad is not
commutative, but only
pseudocommutative
in the sense of
[
HP02
]
.

We now describe the final piece of structure needed for a double category of monoidal double functors.

Definition 5.5

(Monoidal modification)
.

Let
\beta,\beta^{\prime}
be monoidal horizontal transformations and let

\sigma,\tau
be pseudomonoidal vertical transformations, as displayed on the boundary of:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G^{\prime}\mathrlap{.}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\beta}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\rotatebox[origin]{-90.0}{$\Rrightarrow$}{\gamma}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\beta^{\prime}}

\gamma

We now provide an analogue of
3.9
in the monoidal setting, by constructing a double category of monoidal double functors between two monoidal
double categories
\mathbb{C}
and
\mathbb{D}
. It would be routine to construct
a double category of lax monoidal double functors, monoidal vertical transformations, monoidal horizontal
transformations, and monoidal modifications; however, because we wish to involve
pseudomonoidal
vertical transformations, a little more care is needed in checking the details.

Proposition 5.6

(Functor double categories, monoidal case)
.

Let
\mathbb{C}
,

\mathbb{D}
be monoidal double categories. There is a double category

\mathsf{MonDblCat}[\mathbb{C},\mathbb{D}]

of lax monoidal (pseudo) double functors, pseudomonoidal vertical transformations,
monoidal horizontal transformations, and monoidal modifications.

Note that in
3.9
, we considered
oplax
double functors; here we consider only (pseudo) double functors, but endowed with
lax
monoidal structure. While it certainly would be possible to consider “lax monoidal oplax double functors”, this is not needed for our applications.

Proof.

We first show that lax monoidal double functors and pseudomonoidal
vertical transformations form a category. Given pseudomonoidal vertical transformations
\sigma\colon F\Rightarrow F^{\prime}
and
\tau\colon F^{\prime}\Rightarrow F^{\prime\prime}
, we endow the composite vertical
transformation
\tau\cdot\sigma\colon F\Rightarrow F^{\prime\prime}

with pseudomonoidal structure via the pasting composites:

(42)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F{X_{1}}\otimes F{X_{2}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F{X_{1}}\otimes F{X_{2}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F{X_{1}}\otimes F{X_{2}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F({X_{1}}\otimes{X_{2}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F^{\prime}{X_{1}}\otimes F^{\prime}{X_{2}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F^{\prime}{X_{1}}\otimes F^{\prime}{X_{2}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F^{\prime}({X_{1}}\otimes{X_{2}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F^{\prime}({X_{1}}\otimes{X_{2}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F^{\prime\prime}{X_{1}}\otimes F^{\prime\prime}{X_{2}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F^{\prime\prime}({X_{1}}\otimes{X_{2}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F^{\prime\prime}({X_{1}}\otimes{X_{2}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F^{\prime\prime}({X_{1}}\otimes{X_{2}})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F^{2}_{{X_{1}},{X_{2}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\sigma^{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma_{X_{1}}\otimes\sigma_{X_{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma_{X_{1}}\otimes\sigma_{X_{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma_{{X_{1}}\otimes{X_{2}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F^{\prime 2}_{{X_{1}},{X_{2}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\tau^{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau_{X_{1}}\otimes\tau_{X_{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau_{{X_{1}}\otimes{X_{2}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau_{{X_{1}}\otimes{X_{2}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F^{\prime\prime 2}_{{X_{1}},{X_{2}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}}

Proposition 5.7
.

A pseudomonoidal vertical transformation
\sigma\colon F\Rightarrow F^{\prime}
has a companion as a vertical 1-cell of
\mathsf{MonDblCat}[\mathbb{C},\mathbb{D}]
if and only if the underlying vertical
transformation of
\sigma
has a companion as a vertical 1-cell of

\mathsf{DblCat}[\mathbb{C},\mathbb{D}]
, i.e. it is special.

\sigma
has a companion in
\mathsf{MonDblCat}[\mathbb{C},\mathbb{D}]
, then applying the forgetful double functor
\mathsf{MonDblCat}[\mathbb{C},\mathbb{D}]\rightarrow\mathsf{DblCat}[\mathbb{C},\mathbb{D}]
shows it has a companion in
\mathsf{DblCat}[\mathbb{C},\mathbb{D}]

6.
Monoids in monoidal double categories

In this section, we consider horizontal and vertical monoids in a monoidal double category.
When instantiated in the monoidal double categories
\mathsf{DblCat}[\mathbb{C},\mathbb{C}]
and
\mathsf{MonDblCat}[\mathbb{C},\mathbb{C}]
of

3.9
and
5.6
, these will give us the notions of horizontal and vertical double monad, and of monoidal
horizontal and vertical double monad respectively, to be considered in
Sections

7
and
8
.

We begin with the notion of a horizontal monoid in a monoidal double category. This
is analogous to a pseudomonoid in a monoidal bicategory, in that the
associativity and unit axioms do not hold on the nose, but rather up to invertible squares.

Definition 6.1
.

Let
\mathbb{C}
be a monoidal double category. A
horizontal monoid
in
\mathbb{C}

consists of:

•

an object
A
;

•

horizontal 1-cells
m\colon A\otimes A\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow A
and
e\colon I\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow A
;

•

invertible cells

(43)
