Remark 6.2
.

As discussed in
Section

4
, under fairly mild conditions the horizontal bicategory
\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{C})
of a monoidal double category
\mathbb{C}
will have the structure of a monoidal double category, whose monoidal associativity and unit constraint
1
-cells are the companions of the corresponding constraints for
\mathbb{C}
. In this situation, horizontal monoids in
\mathbb{C}
correspond to pseudomonoids in
\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{C})
by taking the companion transposes of the coherence data (
43
).

Definition 6.3

(Vertical monoid)
.

Let
\mathbb{C}
be a monoidal double category. A
vertical monoid
in
\mathbb{C}
is a monoid in the monoidal
category
\mathbb{C}_{0}
. Explicitly, it is an object
A

endowed with vertical 1-cells
m\colon A\otimes A\rightarrow A

and
e\colon I\rightarrow A
satisfying the usual associativity and unit
laws.

The next result shows how we may induce horizontal monoids from vertical ones, and will be applied in
7.4
, relating
horizontal and vertical double monads, and
8.4
, relating monoidal horizontal and vertical double monads.

Theorem 6.4
.

Let
\mathbb{C}
be a monoidal double category and
(A,m,e)
be a vertical
monoid in
\mathbb{C}
, such that
m
and
e
have companions. The companion transposes

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(A\otimes A)\otimes A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\otimes A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\otimes(A\otimes A)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\otimes A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\mathfrak{a}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{m}\otimes\mathrm{id}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{m}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}\otimes\widehat{m}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{m}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\otimes I}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\otimes A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow{\mathfrak{r}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}\otimes\widehat{e}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{m}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I\otimes A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\otimes A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{e}\otimes\mathrm{id}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow{\mathfrak{l}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lambda}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{m}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}}

of the monoid identities endow
(A,\widehat{m},\widehat{e})
with the
structure of a horizontal pseudomonoid.

Proof.

The displayed
2
-morphisms are
constructed using transpose operations like
Eq.

12
from the vertical associativity and unitality monoid
axioms for
A
. They are vertically invertible since
\alpha
,
\rho
and
\lambda
are, so that
\mathfrak{a}^{\textrm{-}1}
may be constructed as
companion transposes of the identities
m\circ(1\otimes m)\circ\alpha^{\textrm{-}1}=m\circ(m\otimes 1)
, and similarly for
\mathfrak{l}^{\textrm{-}1}

and
\mathfrak{r}^{\textrm{-}1}
.

The coherence axioms of
6.1
for a horizontal pseudomonoid
can now be checked by computing appropriate transposes of the
required diagrams and making use of
3.12
.
∎

7.
Double monads

For an ordinary category
\mathsf{C}
, the category of endofunctors of
\mathsf{C}
has a monoidal structure given by composition, and a monoid therein is precisely a monad on
\mathsf{C}
.
In the case of double categories, we can do something similar by exploiting our work in
Sections

3
and
6
, so leading to a notion of double monad: or rather,
two
notions of double monad, horizontal and vertical.

To begin with, observe that
3.9
states in particular that for any double category
\mathbb{C}
, there is a double category

\mathsf{DblCat}[\mathbb{C},\mathbb{C}]
of double endofunctors, vertical transformations, horizontal transformations and modifications
(
3.1
,
3.5
,
3.4
and
3.8
). In fact, as is well-known, this double category is monoidal:

Proposition 7.1

(Composition monoidal structure)
.

Let
\mathbb{C}
be a double category. The double category
\mathsf{DblCat}[\mathbb{C},\mathbb{C}]
admits a monoidal structure given by composition.

Proof.

We only sketch the proof; for a full treatment see, for example,
[
Gar06a
, Proposition 39]
.

Given double endofunctors
F_{1},F_{2}\colon\mathbb{C}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}
, we define
F_{1}\otimes F_{2}
to be the double endofunctor
F_{2}F_{1}
with underlying ordinary functors
(F_{2})_{0}\circ(F_{1})_{0}\colon\mathbb{C}_{0}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{0}
and
(F_{2})_{1}\circ(F_{1})_{1}\colon\mathbb{C}_{1}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}_{1}
, and with coherence data obtained by vertically pasting those for
F
and
G
. Given vertical transformations
\sigma_{1}\colon F_{1}\Rightarrow F^{\prime}_{1}
and

\sigma_{2}\colon F_{2}\Rightarrow F^{\prime}_{2}
, we define
\sigma_{1}\otimes\sigma_{2}
to be the vertical transformation
\sigma_{2}\sigma_{1}\colon F_{2}F_{1}\Rightarrow F^{\prime}_{2}F^{\prime}_{1}
with underlying ordinary natural transformations given by the horizontal composites
(\sigma_{2})_{0}\ast(\sigma_{1})_{0}
and
(\sigma_{2})_{0}\ast(\sigma_{1})_{0}
. With the identity double functor as unit, this yields a strict monoidal structure on the category of double endofunctors and vertical transformations.

By looking at horizontal and vertical monoids (as introduced in
6.1
and
6.3
) in the endofunctor double category, we obtaine notions of
horizontal
and
vertical double monad
. These notions differ by the direction of the transformations
for the the multiplication and unit and by their strictness: a horizontal monad induces a pseudomonad on the horizontal bicategory, while a vertical monad induces a
2
-monad on the vertical
2
-category. We shall relate these notions in
7.4
.

A horizontal double monad is exactly the structure we need to define a horizontal Kleisli double category, as we shall do in
9.1
below. However,
horizontal double monads involves non-trivial coherence axioms for associativity and unit; it is
therefore useful in practice to have some ways of constructing them from simpler kinds of data. For this purpose,
we recall from
[
GP04
, §7]
the following definition:

Definition 7.3

(Vertical double monad)
.

Let
\mathbb{C}
be a double category.

A
vertical double monad
on

\mathbb{C}
is a vertical monoid in
\mathsf{DblCat}[\mathbb{C},\mathbb{C}]
.
Explicitly, it consists of the following data:

•

a double endofunctor
T\colon\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}
;

•

a vertical transformation
m\colon TT\Rightarrow T
, with components
m_{X}\colon TTX\to TX
and

(52)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces TTX}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces TTY}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces TX}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces TY}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces TTM}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces m_{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow m_{M}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces m_{Y}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces TM}

for each object
X
and horizontal 1-cell
M\colon X\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow Y
;

•

a vertical transformation
e\colon 1\Rightarrow T
, with components
e_{X}\colon X\to TX
and

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces TY}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e_{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow e_{M}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e_{Y}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces TM}

for each object
X
and horizontal 1-cell
M\colon X\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow Y
.

These data are required to satisfy associativity and unitality conditions, as in
6.3
.

The notion of a vertical monad is stricter than that of a horizontal monad and thus easier to exhibit in examples.
Once we have a vertical monad, the following result allows us to enhance it to a horizontal one.

Theorem 7.4
.

Let
\mathbb{C}
be a double category and
T\colon\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}
be a vertical double
monad. Assume that its multiplication
m\colon TT\Rightarrow T
and unit
e\colon 1_{\mathbb{C}}\Rightarrow T
are
special vertical transformations. Then
T
induces a
horizontal double monad
(T,\widehat{m},\widehat{e})
on
\mathbb{C}
.

Proof.

If we consider
T
as a vertical monoid in
\mathsf{DblCat}[\mathbb{C},\mathbb{C}]
,
6.4
ensures that it induces a horizontal
monoid therein (namely a horizontal double monad) whenever the unit
e
and multiplication
m
have companions as vertical transformations. By
3.10
, this
will happen if and only if they are special.
∎

While a direct proof of
7.4
would
certainly be possible, the more abstract approach we take has the
advantage of being equally applicable to the case of
monoidal

double monads (
8.4
), for which a direct approach seems less
practicable. It is to this that we now turn.

8.
Monoidal double monads

In this section, we retread the material of the previous section in the context of
monoidal
double categories, leading to the
notions of a monoidal horizontal and monoidal vertical double monad, and results relating the two. In
Section

9
, we will exploit
these
notions in order to impose monoidal structure on the Kleisli double category of a horizontal double monad.

As a first step, we show that when
\mathbb{C}
is a monoidal double category, we can extend the composition monoidal structure on the endofunctor
double category
\mathsf{DblCat}[\mathbb{C},\mathbb{C}]
as recalled in
7.1
, to a monoidal structure on the
monoidal

endofunctor double category
\mathsf{MonDblCat}[\mathbb{C},\mathbb{C}]
of
5.6
.

Proposition 8.1

(Composition monoidal structure on
\mathsf{MonDblCat}[\mathbb{C},\mathbb{C}]
)
.

Let
\mathbb{C}
be a monoidal double category. The composition monoidal structure of the double category
\mathsf{DblCat}[\mathbb{C},\mathbb{C}]
lifts to a monoidal structure on the double category

\mathsf{MonDblCat}[\mathbb{C},\mathbb{C}]
of monoidal endofunctors,
pseudomonoidal

vertical transformations, monoidal horizontal transformations and monoidal modifications.

Proof.

We must lift each of the pieces of data exhibited in the proof
of
7.1
to the monoidal context.
We first lift the strict monoidal structure on the category of
0
-cells and vertical
1
-cells.
If
F_{1},F_{2}\colon\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}
are lax
monoidal double endofunctors of
\mathbb{C}
, then their composite

F_{2}F_{1}
bears lax monoidal structure with vertical
1
-cell components

\displaystyle(F_{2}F_{1})^{2}_{{X_{1}},{X_{2}}}

\displaystyle=F_{2}F_{1}{X_{1}}\otimes F_{2}F_{1}{X_{2}}\xrightarrow{F_{2}^{2}}F_{2}(F_{1}{X_{1}}\otimes F_{1}{X_{2}})\xrightarrow{F_{2}F_{1}^{2}}F_{2}F_{1}({X_{1}}\otimes{X_{2}}),

\displaystyle(F_{2}F_{1})^{0}

\displaystyle=I\xrightarrow{F_{2}^{0}}F_{2}I\xrightarrow{F_{2}F_{1}^{0}}F_{2}F_{1}I

and
2
-morphism components given similarly by

(F_{2}F_{1})^{2}_{M,N}=F_{2}(F_{1}^{2})_{M,N}\cdot(F_{2}^{2})_{F_{1}M,F_{1}N}
.
Next, if
{\sigma_{1}\colon F_{1}\Rightarrow F_{1}^{\prime}}
and

\sigma_{2}\colon F_{2}\Rightarrow F_{2}^{\prime}
are pseudomonoidal vertical
transformations, then the composite vertical transformation
\sigma_{2}\sigma_{1}\colon F_{2}F_{1}\Rightarrow F_{2}^{\prime}F_{1}^{\prime}

bears pseudomonoidal structure witnessed by the
2
-morphisms

(\sigma_{2}\sigma_{1})^{2}{=}\hbox to491.78pt{\vbox to159.08pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 245.88893pt\lower-79.20793pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@closescope \hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {}{}{}{{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{}{{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{}{}{{

where the empty squares are horizontal identities
existing due to naturality of
\sigma_{2}
and
F_{2}^{\prime 2}
. It is direct to check that these pseudomonoidal constraint cells are stable under vertical
composition, so that we have a functorial tensor product on the category of lax monoidal functors and pseudomonoidal vertical transformations.
Taking this tensor product together with the (strict) monoidal

1_{\mathbb{C}}
as unit, we obtain a strict monoidal category: indeed, for any lax
monoidal double endofunctors
F_{3},F_{2},F_{1}
of
\mathbb{C}
,
(F_{3}F_{2})F_{1}=F_{3}(F_{2}F_{1})
as lax monoidal double
functors, since both have coherence vertical
1
-cells given by

F_{3}F_{2}F_{1}{X_{1}}\otimes F_{3}F_{2}F_{1}{X_{2}}\xrightarrow{F_{3}^{2}}F_{3}(F_{2}F_{1}{X_{1}}\otimes F_{2}F_{1}{X_{2}})\xrightarrow{F_{3}F_{2}^{2}}F_{3}F_{2}(F_{1}{X_{1}}\otimes F_{1}{X_{2}})\xrightarrow{F_{3}F_{2}F_{1}^{2}}F_{3}F_{2}F_{1}({X_{1}}\otimes{X_{2}})\mathrlap{,}

using the fact that double functors strictly preserve vertical composition; and
correspondingly for the coherence
2
-morphisms.

Moreover, given monoidal modifications
\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2}
as in
Eq.

45
, their composite

\gamma_{2}\gamma_{1}\colon\beta_{2}\beta_{1}\Rrightarrow\beta_{2}^{\prime}\beta_{1}^{\prime}
given by (
46
) can be verified to satisfy the axioms

Eq.

41
that render it monoidal, using, among other things, the monoidality of
\gamma_{1}
and
\gamma_{2}
. The functoriality of this tensor
product is now inherited from
\mathsf{DblCat}[\mathbb{C},\mathbb{C}]_{1}
, given that monoidality is a mere condition on a modification. It is moreover easy to
check that the associativity and unitality modifications in
\mathsf{DblCat}[\mathbb{C},\mathbb{C}]_{1}
become monoidal on lifting them to

\mathsf{MonDblCat}[\mathbb{C},\mathbb{C}]_{1}
, so providing the last pieces of data for the desired monoidal structure.

It remains to lift
\tau
and
\eta
from
\mathsf{DblCat}[\mathbb{C},\mathbb{C}]
to
\mathsf{MonDblCat}[\mathbb{C},\mathbb{C}]
: and this is again simply a matter of checking that the modifications obtained from
\mathsf{DblCat}[\mathbb{C},\mathbb{C}]
do indeed become monoidal modifications.
∎

Using this result, and paralleling the developments of
Section

7
, we can now give succinct definitions of the notions
of monoidal horizontal and vertical double monad.

Definition 8.2

(Monoidal horizontal double monad)
.

Let
\mathbb{C}
be a monoidal double category.
A
monoidal horizontal double monad
on
\mathbb{C}
is a horizontal monoid in the monoidal double category
\mathsf{MonDblCat}[\mathbb{C},\mathbb{C}]
.
Explicitly, it is a horizontal double monad
(T,m,e)
on
\mathbb{C}
in the sense of
7.2
such that:

•

the double functor
T\colon\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}
is lax monoidal,
i.e.
, it comes equipped with structure vertical 1-cells
T^{2}_{X_{1},X_{2}}\colon TX_{1}\otimes TX_{2}\to T(X_{1}\otimes X_{2})
,
T^{0}\colon I\to TI
and 2-morphisms

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces TX_{1}\otimes TX_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces TY_{1}\otimes TY_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T(X_{1}\otimes X_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T(Y_{1}\otimes Y_{2})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T^{2}_{X_{1},X_{2}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow T^{2}_{M,N}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces TM\otimes TN}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T^{2}_{Y_{1},Y_{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T(M\otimes N)}

satisfying the axioms of
5.1
;

•

the horizontal transformation

While a direct proof of
8.4
should be possible, the construction of all the data for a monoidal horizontal double monad from that of a
pseudomonoidal vertical double monad using companions, let alone the verification of the coherence axioms, would be a daunting task. It is at this point that the advantage of our abstract view becomes clear;
as an added bonus, the proofs of
7.4
and
8.4

become essentially the same.

9.
Monoidal Kleisli double categories

In this section, we first introduce the (horizontal) Kleisli double category
{\mathbb{K}\mathsf{l}}(T)
for a
horizontal double monad
T
(
7.2
) on a double category
\mathbb{C}
, with a particularly important case being where
T
is induced from a vertical double monad (
7.3
) as in
7.4
.

We next consider what happens when the double category
\mathbb{C}
is monoidal and the double monad
T
is also monoidal. We would naturally expect the monoidal structure of
\mathbb{C}
to extend to
{\mathbb{K}\mathsf{l}}(T)
, just as happens with an ordinary monoidal monad on an ordinary monoidal category. However, because the monoidal constraint data for a horizontal double monad does not point exclusively in the horizontal direction, things are slightly more subtle. To even obtain monoidal structure we must assume certain companions exist, and even then, this structure is only
oplax
monoidal in general (
9.4
). Again, the situation where
T
is induced from a vertical double monad will be important, and in this special case, we describe sufficient conditions for this oplax monoidal structure on
{\mathbb{K}\mathsf{l}}(T)
to be normal oplax (
9.7
) or (pseudo) monoidal (
9.8
).

We begin with the construction of the horizontal Kleisli double category of a horizontal double monad. This construction is essentially contained in
[
CS10
]
; there, the authors start from a
vertical
double monad
(T,m,e)
, and define from it a
horizontal
Kleisli double category (Definition 4.1 of
op. cit.
) which in general is only a so-called
virtual
double category. These are weaker structures than double categories, in which horizontal
1
-cells do not compose, but instead are formed into a structure of “multi-
2
-morphisms”; however,
[
CS10
, Theorem A.8]
shows that, when the vertical transformations
e\colon 1\Rightarrow T
and
m\colon TT\Rightarrow T
are
special
, this virtual double category is in fact a double category. In this case, the horizontal Kleisli double category of
loc. cit.
can be obtained as follows: first apply
7.4
to form the horizontal double monad
(T,\widehat{m},\widehat{e})
associated to
(T,m,e)
; and then apply the following result.

Theorem 9.1
.

Let
\mathbb{C}
be a double category and
(T,m,e)
be a horizontal double monad on it.
There is a double category
{\mathbb{K}\mathsf{l}}(T)
, called the
horizontal Kleisli double category
of
\mathbb{C}
, wherein:

•

objects
are objects of
\mathbb{C}
;

•

vertical 1-cells
are vertical 1-cells of
\mathbb{C}
;

•

are
horizontal 1-cells

of
\mathbb{C}
;

•

as to the left below, are the 2-morphisms of
\mathbb{C}
as to the right:

Vertical composition in

is the same as in

We have not ascribed any kind of universal property to the construction of the Kleisli double category, and for our purposes we do not need to; however, if we were to do so, then, following
[
Str72
]
, we would express it in terms of
universal opalgebra
structure on the canonical embedding of
\mathbb{C}
into
{\mathbb{K}\mathsf{l}}(T)
:

Definition 9.2
.

Let
\mathbb{C}
be a double category and
(T,m,e)
be a horizontal double monad on it. The
canonical embedding

F_{T}\colon\mathbb{C}\rightarrow{\mathbb{K}\mathsf{l}}(T)
is the double functor which is the identity on objects and vertical
1
-cells; sends a horizontal
1
-cell
M\colon X\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow Y
to
e_{Y}\circ M\colon X\rightsquigarrow Y
, and correspondingly for 2-morphisms between horizontal
1
-cells.

Applying
3.3
to this canonical embedding, we immediately obtain the following result concerning companions in Kleisli double categories (
cf.

[
CS10
, Proposition 7.5]
):

Proposition 9.3
.

Let
\mathbb{C}
be a double category,
T
a horizontal double monad on
\mathbb{C}
, and

f\colon X\to X^{\prime}
a vertical 1-cell of
\mathbb{C}
. If
f
has a companion as a vertical 1-cell of
\mathbb{C}
, then it
has a companion also as a vertical 1-cell of
{\mathbb{K}\mathsf{l}}(T)
. ∎

We now consider the Kleisli double category when
\mathbb{C}
is a monoidal double category and
T
is a monoidal horizontal double monad (
8.2
). As discussed above, it does not seem to be true in general that the monoidal structure of
\mathbb{C}
will extend to
{\mathbb{K}\mathsf{l}}(T)
; however, under mild assumptions which
are satisfied in our applications, we do obtain at least an oplax monoidal structure (
4.1
) on
{\mathbb{K}\mathsf{l}}(T)
:

Theorem 9.4
.

Let
\mathbb{C}
be a monoidal double category and
T
a
monoidal horizontal double monad on
\mathbb{C}
. If the vertical 1-cell
T^{0}\colon I\rightarrow TI
and each vertical
1
-cell

T^{2}_{X_{1},X_{2}}\colon TX_{1}\otimes TX_{2}\rightarrow T(X_{1}\otimes X_{2})

has a
companion, then the monoidal structure of
\mathbb{C}
induces an oplax monoidal structure on
{\mathbb{K}\mathsf{l}}(T)
.

With some effort, one may show that with these structure cells, the horizontal double
Kleisli category
{\mathbb{K}\mathsf{l}}(T)
is an oplax monoidal double category in the sense of

4.1
. We do not provide the details here, but in
Section

A.2
we give some sample verifications, along with a number of technical lemmas used repeatedly in the calculations.
∎

It is very natural to ask when the oplax monoidal structure of the preceding definition is in fact a genuine (pseudo) monoidal structure, or at least a
normal
oplax monoidal structure. For our purposes, we will only answer this question in the case of primary interest, where our monoidal horizontal monad is induced from a pseudomonoidal vertical monad (
8.3
). To start with, putting together
8.4
and
9.4
gives us:

Corollary 9.5
.

Let
\mathbb{C}
be a monoidal double category and
T
be a pseudomonoidal vertical double monad.
If it is true that:

(1)

the multiplication and unit of
T
are special; and

(2)

all vertical 1-cells
T^{2}_{X_{1},X_{2}}\colon TX_{1}\otimes TX_{2}\rightarrow T(X_{1}\otimes X_{2})
and

T^{0}\colon I\rightarrow TI
have
companions,

then the Kleisli double category
{\mathbb{K}\mathsf{l}}(T)
of the induced
monoidal horizontal monad
(T,\widehat{m},\widehat{e})
admits an oplax monoidal structure found as in
9.4
. ∎

Remark 9.6
.

Notice that in the situation of the above corollary, it is only the interchange
2
-morphisms
\tau
of the oplax monoidal structure which may not be invertible. Indeed, each of the other structure 2-morphisms
\eta,\delta,\iota
, as displayed
in (
63
) and (
64
), must be invertible; for example, in this case
\eta
is the transpose of the
2
-morphism

Eq.

58
which is, in turn, the transpose of the
\mathsf{V}(\mathbb{C})
-invertible
2
-morphism
e^{2}

Eq.

57
of the pseudomonoidal
vertical transformation
e
, and as such, is invertible by
2.9
6
.

9.5

{\mathbb{K}\mathsf{l}}(T)

4.3

[
HP02

as in
8.3
a vertical double transformation
\kappa\colon({\mathord{\text{--}}})\otimes T(\mathord{?})\Rightarrow T\circ({\mathord{\text{--}}}\otimes\mathord{?})
called the
strength

T^{2}\circ(e\otimes 1)
with components

In an analogous way, we can also define the
costrength
as a vertical transformation
T({\mathord{\text{--}}})\otimes(\mathord{?})\Rightarrow T\circ({\mathord{\text{--}}}\otimes\mathord{?})
. It turns out that requiring these two
vertical transformations to be special, as in
3.6
, is sufficient to make the oplax monoidal structure on
{\mathbb{K}\mathsf{l}}(T)
normal:

Proposition 9.7
.

Let
\mathbb{C}
be a monoidal double category and
T
be a pseudomonoidal vertical double monad.
If it is true that:

(1)

the multiplication and unit of
T
are special;

(2)

all vertical 1-cells
T^{2}_{X_{1},X_{2}}\colon TX_{1}\otimes TX_{2}\rightarrow T(X_{1}\otimes X_{2})
and
T^{0}\colon I\rightarrow TI
have
companions; and

(3)

the strength and costrength of
T
are special vertical transformations,

then the oplax monoidal double structure on
{\mathbb{K}\mathsf{l}}(T)
found as in
9.5
is normal.

Proof.

We need to verify that each oplax double functor
X_{1}\boxtimes({\mathord{\text{--}}})\colon{\mathbb{K}\mathsf{l}}(T)\to{\mathbb{K}\mathsf{l}}(T)
and
({\mathord{\text{--}}})\boxtimes X_{2}\colon{\mathbb{K}\mathsf{l}}(T)\to{\mathbb{K}\mathsf{l}}(T)
is in fact a (pseudo)
double functor. By
9.6
, we already know
that the square
\eta
in
Eq.

63
is invertible, which expresses the invertibility of the identity constraints for these
double functors. As for the binary functoriality constraints, it suffices by symmetry to consider the case of
X_{1}\boxtimes({\mathord{\text{--}}})
. To say that its binary constraints are invertible is to say that the
2
-morphism in
Eq.

62
is
invertible
when

X=X_{1}=Y_{1}=Z_{1}
and
M_{1}=N_{1}=\widehat{e}_{X_{1}}
. The
2
-morphism in question is given by:

(66)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{1}\otimes X_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces TX_{1}\otimes TZ_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T(X_{1}\otimes Z_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{1}\otimes X_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces TX_{1}\otimes TY_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces TTX_{1}\otimes TTZ_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces TX_{1}\otimes TZ_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T(X_{1}\otimes Z_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{1}\otimes X_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces TX_{1}\otimes TY_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces TTX_{1}\otimes TTZ_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T(TX_{1}\otimes TZ_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces TT(X_{1}\otimes Z_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T(X_{1}\otimes Z_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{1}\otimes X_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces TX_{1}\otimes TY_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T(X_{1}\otimes Y_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T(TX_{1}\otimes TZ_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces TT(X_{1}\otimes Z_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T(X_{1}\otimes Z_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{1}\otimes X_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces TX_{1}\otimes TY_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T(X_{1}\otimes Y_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces TT(X_{1}\otimes Z_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T(X_{1}\otimes Z_{2})\mathrlap{.}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\cong}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\widehat{m}\circ T\widehat{e}\circ\widehat{e})\otimes(\widehat{m}\circ TN_{2}\circ M_{2})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{T^{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{e}\otimes M_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T\widehat{e}\otimes TN_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\widehat{m}^{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{m}\otimes\widehat{m}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{T^{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{e}\otimes M_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T\widehat{e}\otimes TN_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\widehat{T^{2}_{\mathstrut}}\!\!\!\!{\mathstrut}_{\widehat{e},N_{2}}\hskip 8.19447pt}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{T^{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T\widehat{T^{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{m}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{e}\otimes M_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{T^{2}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\cong}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T(\widehat{e}\otimes N_{2})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T\widehat{T^{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{m}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{e}\otimes M_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{T^{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T(\widehat{T^{2}}\circ(\widehat{e}\otimes N_{2}))}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{m}}

Clearly the first and final rows of this diagram are invertible. On the second row, the
2
-morphism
\widehat{m^{2}}
corresponds under transpose to the
\mathsf{V}(\mathbb{C})
-invertible cell
m^{2}
of the pseudomonoidal vertical
transformation
m
in
Eq.

56
, and as such is invertible by
2.9
6
. Thus, we will be done if we can also prove the invertibility of the third row of the diagram.

Now, since the strength
Eq.

65
is by assumption a special vertical transformation, it is in particular true that the companion transpose of the component

\kappa_{\widehat{e},N_{2}}
is
invertible. This transpose is equally well the composite:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{1}\otimes TY_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces TX_{1}\otimes TTZ_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces TTX_{1}\otimes TTZ_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T(TX_{1}\otimes TZ_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{1}\otimes TY_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces TX_{1}\otimes TY_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces TTX_{1}\otimes TTZ_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T(TX_{1}\otimes TZ_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X\otimes TY_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces TX\otimes TY_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T(X_{1}\otimes Y_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T(TX_{2}\otimes TZ_{2})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{e}\otimes TN_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow(*)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{e}T\otimes 1}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{T^{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{e}\otimes 1}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T\widehat{e}\otimes TN_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\widehat{T^{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{T^{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{e}\otimes 1}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{T^{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T(\widehat{e}\otimes N_{2})}

where the
2
-morphism
(*)
on the top row is the transpose of the 2-cell
e_{\widehat{e}_{X_{1}}}\otimes 1_{N_{2}}
. But by
3.12
, this
(*)
is itself the transpose of a vertical identity, and as such, is invertible by
2.9
6
. It follows that the composite
2
-morphism comprising the bottom row of this diagram is invertible, which now implies the invertibility of the third row of (
66
) as desired.
∎

Although this will not be the case in our applications, we note in particular the following sufficient conditions for the induced oplax monoidal structure on
{\mathbb{K}\mathsf{l}}(T)
to be not just normal oplax, but in fact a genuine (pseudo) monoidal structure.

Corollary 9.8
.

Let
\mathbb{C}
be a monoidal double category and
T
be a pseudomonoidal vertical double monad.
If it is true that:

(1)

the multiplication and unit of
T
are special;

(2)

all vertical 1-cells
T^{2}_{X_{1},X_{2}}\colon TX_{1}\otimes TX_{2}\rightarrow T(X_{1}\otimes X_{2})
and
T^{0}\colon I\rightarrow TI
have
companions; and

(3)

the monoidality constraint
T^{2}
of
T
is a special vertical transformation,

then the oplax monoidal double structure on
{\mathbb{K}\mathsf{l}}(T)
found as in
9.5
is genuinely monoidal.

Proof.

\eta
,
\delta
and
\iota
are already known to be invertible, and, arguing as before, the assumption that
T^{2}
is special ensures that
every
component (
62
) of the oplax monoidal interchange
\tau
is invertible.
∎

In the situation of
9.7
, the fact that

{\mathbb{K}\mathsf{l}}(T)
is a normal oplax monoidal double category implies that its
horizontal bicategory inherits the monoidal structure, in the sense
specified in
4.9
. We thus obtain the following result as the culmination of the abstract development of the paper thus far.
This will be the result we use to obtain the monoidal structure on the bicategory of coloured symmetric sequences
in
Section

10
.

Corollary 9.9
.

Let
\mathbb{C}
be a monoidal double category and
T
be a pseudomonoidal vertical double monad. Under the
assumptions of
9.7
, the horizontal bicategory of
{\mathbb{K}\mathsf{l}}(T)
admits a normal oplax monoidal structure.

Proof.

This follows from
4.11
,
9.7
and
9.3
.
∎

10.
The arithmetic product of coloured symmetric sequences

In this section, we apply the theory developed in the previous
sections to our intended application, namely coloured symmetric
sequences. Throughout this section, we fix a cocomplete
cartesian
closed
category
\mathcal{V}
, considered as a symmetric monoidal closed category
with respect to its cartesian closed structure.
The restriction to a cartesian
monoidal structure was already made in
[
DH14
,
GL16
]

and indeed it is essential for some of our results, as we explain further below.

In order to help readers follow our development, let us display the main double categories to be considered
in this section in a commutative diagram of inclusions:

\begin{gathered}\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 15.34033pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-14.99309pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 48.54868pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}_{\mathcal{V}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 63.80566pt\raise-23.94443pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern-15.34033pt\raise-31.38887pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 39.34033pt\raise-31.38887pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 39.34033pt\raise-31.38887pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}\mathrlap{.}}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces\end{gathered}

On the left-hand side of the diagram,
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
is the double category
of matrices of
2.4
and
\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
is the double category of profunctors of
2.5
. On the right-hand side of the
diagram,
\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}
is the double category of categorical symmetric sequences which arises from
\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
as a Kleisli double category,
and
\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}_{\mathcal{V}}
is its full double subcategory spanned by discrete
\mathcal{V}
-categories—much like the double category
\mathbb{M}\mathsf{at}_{\mathcal{V}}
is a full
double subcategory of
\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
. We will define the double categories
\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}
and
\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}_{\mathcal{V}}
explicitly in
10.5
, but in order to do so, we must first introduce
the relevant double monad for the Kleisli construction.

Let
X
be a small
\mathcal{V}
-category. For

n\in\mathbb{N}
, let us define the
\mathcal{V}
-category
S_{n}(X)
as follows. The objects of
S_{n}(X)

are
n
-tuples
\vec{x}=(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})
of objects of
X
. Given
two such
n
-tuples
\vec{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})
and
\vec{x}^{\prime}=(x^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,x^{\prime}_{n})
,
the hom-object of maps between them is defined by

S_{n}(X)[\vec{x},\vec{x}^{\prime}]\mathrel{\mathop{:}}=\bigsqcup_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\bigsqcap_{1\leq i\leq n}X[x_{\sigma(i)},x^{\prime}_{i}]

where
\mathfrak{S}_{n}
is the
n
-th symmetric group, and where
\bigsqcup
and
\bigsqcap
denote coproduct and product respectively. We then let
SX
be the following coproduct in
\mathsf{Cat}_{\mathcal{V}}
:

SX=\bigsqcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}S_{n}(X)\mathrlap{.}

The
\mathcal{V}
-category
SX
admits a symmetric strict monoidal structure in which the tensor product, written as
\vec{x},\vec{y}\mapsto\vec{x}\otimes\vec{y}
,
is given by concatenation of sequences; the tensor unit is given by the empty
sequence, written
(\;)
; and the symmetry is given by the evident permutations. The operation
mapping
X
to
SX
extends to a 2-functor
S\colon\mathsf{Cat}_{\mathcal{V}}\to\mathsf{Cat}_{\mathcal{V}}
, which is part of a 2-monad
whose strict algebras are symmetric strict monoidal
\mathcal{V}
-categories. The multiplication of this 2-monad
has components
m_{X}\colon SSX\rightarrow SX
, for
X\in\mathsf{Cat}_{\mathcal{V}}
, defined by taking a list of
lists to its flattening:

m_{X}(\vec{x}^{1},\dots,\vec{x}^{k})\mathrel{\mathop{:}}=\vec{x}^{1}\otimes\ldots\otimes\vec{x}^{k}\mathrlap{.}

The unit of the 2-monad has components
e_{X}\colon X\rightarrow SX
, for
X\in\mathsf{Cat}_{\mathcal{V}}
,
defined by taking an object
x\in X
to the singleton list
(x)\in SX
.

We now show that, firstly,
S
can be made into a vertical double monad on
\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
, and secondly, that this vertical double monad can be turned
into a horizontal double monad. To say that
S
can be made into a vertical double monad is equivalently to say that the underlying
2
-functor of

S
extends along the inclusion of bicategories
\mathsf{Cat}_{\mathcal{V}}\rightarrow\mathsf{Prof}_{\mathcal{V}}
—see Remark
10.2
below—while to say that this vertical monad can be
turned into a horizontal one amounts to saying that the whole
2
-monad
S
extends from
\mathsf{Cat}_{\mathcal{V}}
to
\mathsf{Prof}_{\mathcal{V}}
. This is a known
result, and there are two approaches in the literature to proving it. The first uses the theory of pseudo-distributive laws; see, for
example
[
FGHW18
]
. The second, which we follow here, is essentially a categorification of the approach of
[
Bar70
]
.

Proposition 10.1
.

The free symmetric strict monoidal category
2
-monad
S
on
\mathsf{Cat}_{\mathcal{V}}
extends in an essentially unique way to a vertical double monad on

\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
. The multiplication and unit vertical transformations of this double monad are special.

Here, we say that a vertical double monad
T
on a double category
\mathbb{C}

extends
a
2
-monad
R
on the vertical
2
-category
\mathsf{V}(\mathbb{C})
, if
R
is isomorphic (as a
2
-monad) to the 2-monad
\mathsf{V}(T)
on
\mathsf{V}(\mathbb{C})
induced by
T
. By saying that an extension of
R
is
essentially unique
, we mean to assert the contractibility of the category in which objects are vertical double monads
T
on
\mathbb{C}
endowed with an isomorphism of
2
-monads
\mathsf{V}(T)\cong R
, and morphisms are vertical double monad morphisms compatible with the isomorphisms to
R
.

Proof.

Because any double functor preserves companions (
3.3
), any extension of
S
to
\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
must satisfy
S(\widehat{F})\cong\widehat{SF}
for a
\mathcal{V}
-functor
F
. Because
\widehat{F}\dashv\widecheck{F}
in
\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}})
, and any double functor preserves adjunctions in
the horizontal bicategory, we must also have
S(\widecheck{F})\cong\widecheck{SF}
. Since by
[
Str80
, §6]
, every

\mathcal{V}
-profunctor
M\colon X\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow Y
admits a globular isomorphism to one of the form
\widecheck{G}\circ\widehat{F}
for a suitable cospan of

\mathcal{V}
-functors
F\colon X\rightarrow Z\leftarrow Y\colon G
, the preceding conditions determine the action of
S
on horizontal

1
-cells of
\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
to within isomorphism. Using this idea, one obtains the following explicit definition: given
M\colon X\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow Y
,
SM\colon SX\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow SY
is defined as the

\mathbb{N}
-indexed coproduct in
(\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}})_{1}
of
S_{n}(M)\colon S_{n}(X)\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow S_{n}(Y)
, where

(67)

S_{n}(M)(\vec{y},\vec{x})\mathrel{\mathop{:}}=\bigsqcup_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\bigsqcap_{1\leq i\leq n}M(y_{\sigma(i)},x_{i})\mathrlap{.}

The action of
S
on
2
-morphisms of
\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
is now forced by
2.9
3
and the fact that any double functor preserves
globularity; the reader will easily guess an explicit formula, and this guess is the correct one. This completes the extension of
S
to a double functor on
\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
; that these data are indeed double functorial is verified, for example, in
[
Gar06b
, Proposition 55]
, to which we refer for further details. Note also that the manner in which we defined the action of
S
on horizontal
1
-cells and
2
-morphisms means that this extension is essentially unique, in the sense set out above.

We now extend the unit
e
and multiplication
m
of the
2
-monad
S
; the missing data are the
2
-morphism components
e_{M}
and
m_{M}

(
52
,
53
) associated to a horizontal
1
-cell
M\colon X\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow Y
. Writing
M\cong\widecheck{G}\circ\widehat{F}
as before, we
see
that

e_{M}
and
m_{M}
are determined by
e_{\widehat{F}}
,
e_{\widecheck{G}}
,
m_{\widehat{F}}
and
m_{\widecheck{G}}
:

(68)

e_{M}=\hbox to148.6pt{\vbox to115.04pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 74.29848pt\lower-58.43474pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@closescope \hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {}{}{}{{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{}{{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}{{}}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{}{}{{

To the left,
3.12
implies that
e_{\widehat{F}}
is the companion transpose of the identity of vertical
1
-cells

e_{Z}\circ F=SF\circ e_{X}
; while a suitable dual of
3.12
implies that
e_{\widecheck{F}}
is the

conjoint
transpose of the identity
e_{Z}\circ G=SG\circ e_{Y}
. In a similar way, the
2
-morphisms
m_{\widehat{F}}
and
m_{\widecheck{G}}

are
forced. An explicit verification that these data satisfy the vertical double monad axioms is, again, given in
[
Gar06b
, Proposition 55]
. So we have extended
S
to a vertical double monad on
\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
; and like before, the manner in which we made this extension forces it to be essentially unique.

, as to the left below, is equally given as to the
right:

(69)

\int^{\vec{y}\in SY}M(z,\vec{y})\times SN(\vec{y},\vec{x})\cong\int^{\vec{y}\in Y^{n}}M(z,\vec{y})\times\bigsqcap_{1\leqslant i\leqslant n}N(y_{i},x_{i})\hbox to0.0pt{ .\hss}

Indeed, we can immediately reduce the left-hand coend to one over
\vec{y}\in S_{n}Y
; and for such a
\vec{y}
, we have
M(z,\vec{y})\times SN(\vec{y},\vec{x})\cong\bigsqcup_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}M(z,\vec{y})\times\bigsqcap_{1\leqslant i\leqslant n}N(y_{\sigma(i)},x_{i})
. On the
\sigma
-summand of
this coproduct, we define the component of the desired isomorphism
Eq.

69
to be

M(z,\vec{y})\times\bigsqcap_{1\leqslant i\leqslant n}N(y_{\sigma(i)},x_{i})\xrightarrow{M(1,\sigma^{\textrm{-}1})\times 1}M(z,\sigma^{\ast}\vec{y})\times\bigsqcap_{1\leqslant i\leqslant n}N(\,(\sigma^{\ast}\vec{y})_{i},x_{i})\hookrightarrow\int^{\vec{y}\in Y^{n}}\!M(z,\vec{y})\times\bigsqcap_{1\leqslant i\leqslant n}N(y_{i},x_{i})

where
(\sigma^{\ast}\vec{y})_{i}=y_{\sigma(i)}
and where
\sigma^{\textrm{-}1}\colon\vec{y}\rightarrow\sigma^{\ast}\vec{y}
is the evident symmetry
isomorphism in
SY
.

We now show that the extended vertical transformations
e
and
m
are special,
i.e.
that the following companion transpose
2
-morphisms are invertible:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces SY}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces SZ}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces SY}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{e}_{Y}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\widehat{e}_{M}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{e}_{Z}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces SM}

and

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces SSZ}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces SSY}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces SY}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces SSZ}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces SZ}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces SY\mathrlap{.}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces SSM}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{m}_{Y}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow\widehat{m}_{M}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{m}_{Z}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces SM}

Starting to the left, let
z\in Z
and
\vec{y}=(y_{1},\dots,y_{n})\in SY
. To within isomorphism, using the formulas for composition and
companions for profunctors (
8
,
11
) as well as
Eq.

67
, the profunctor at the bottom of the
square sends
(\vec{y},z)
to

(70)

SM(\vec{y},(z))=\begin{cases}M(y_{1},z)&\text{if $n=1$;}\\
0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

On the other hand, the profunctor around the top sends
(\vec{y},z)
to:

(71)

\int^{y^{\prime}\in Y}SY[\vec{y},(y^{\prime})]\times M(y^{\prime},z)=\begin{cases}\int^{y^{\prime}\in Y}Y[y_{1},y^{\prime}]\times M(y^{\prime},z)&\text{if $n=1$;}\\
0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

In the only non-trivial case where
n=1
, the comparison
2
-cell

\widehat{e}_{M}
from (
71
) to (
70
) is given by
composition: and this is invertible by the Yoneda lemma.

We proceed similarly for
\widehat{m}_{M}
. Let
\vec{z}=(\vec{z}^{1},\dots,\vec{z}^{n})\in SSZ
with
\vec{z}^{i}=(z_{m_{i\textrm{-}1}+1},\dots,z_{m_{i}})
for some

0=m_{0}\leqslant m_{1}\leqslant\dots\leqslant m_{n}
,
and let
\vec{y}=(y_{1},\dots,y_{m})\in SY
. The only non-trivial case is when
m_{n}=m
so we immediately restrict to that.
This time, the profunctor in the bottom row sends
(\vec{y},\vec{z})
to

(72)

SM(\vec{y},\bigotimes_{1\leqslant i\leqslant n}{\vec{z}}^{\,i})=\bigsqcup_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{m}}\bigsqcap_{1\leqslant i\leqslant m}M(y_{\sigma(m)},z_{m})\mathrlap{.}

On the other hand, the profunctor around the top sends
(\vec{y},\vec{z})
to

(73)

\displaystyle\int^{\vec{w}\in SSY}SY[\vec{y},\bigotimes_{1\leqslant i\leqslant m}\vec{w}^{i}]\times SSM(\vec{w},\vec{z})

\displaystyle\cong\int^{\vec{w}^{1},\dots,\vec{w}^{n}\in SY}SY[\vec{y},\bigotimes_{1\leqslant i\leqslant m}\vec{w}^{i}]\times\bigsqcap_{1\leqslant j\leqslant n}SM(\vec{w}^{j},\vec{z}^{j})

\displaystyle\cong\int^{w_{1},\dots,w_{m}\in Y}SY[\vec{y},\vec{w}]\times\bigsqcap_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leqslant j\leqslant n\\
m_{i\textrm{-}1}+1\leqslant i\leqslant m_{i}\end{subarray}}M(w_{i},z_{i})

\displaystyle\cong\bigsqcup_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{m}}\int^{w_{1},\dots,w_{m}\in Y}\bigsqcap_{1\leqslant i\leqslant m}Y[y_{\sigma(i)},w_{i}]\times M(w_{i},z_{i})\mathrlap{,}

using
Eq.

69
once at the first step, and
n
times at the second step.
The comparison
2
-morphism
\widehat{m}_{M}
from (
73
) to (
72
) is again given by composition, and this is again invertible by the Yoneda
lemma.
∎

Remark 10.2
.

In fact, the above argument shows that,
any

2
-monad
R
on
\mathsf{Cat}_{\mathcal{V}}
which extends to
\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
will have an essentially-unique such extension; for indeed, the action on horizontal
1
-cells must be given as
R(M)=\widecheck{RG}\circ\widehat{RF}
, where
M=\widecheck{G}\circ\widehat{F}
, and the components of the extended unit and multiplication at a horizontal
1
-cell
M
must be determined similarly. The only non-trivial point is verifying that composition of horizontal
1
-cells is preserved to within globular isomorphism—and this comes to the same thing as asking that the underlying
2
-functor of
R
extends along the homomorphism of bicategories
\widehat{({\mathord{\text{--}}})}\colon\mathsf{Cat}_{\mathcal{V}}\rightarrow\mathrm{Prof}_{\mathcal{V}}
. Thus, to give an extension of the
2
-monad
R
to
\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
is equally to give an extension of the underlying
2
-functor along
\widehat{({\mathord{\text{--}}})}\colon\mathsf{Cat}_{\mathcal{V}}\rightarrow\mathrm{Prof}_{\mathcal{V}}
, as claimed above.

Corollary 10.3
.

The
2
-monad
S\colon\mathsf{Cat}_{\mathcal{V}}\to\mathsf{Cat}_{\mathcal{V}}
induces a horizontal double monad
S\colon\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
.

Proof.

Apply
7.4
to the vertical double monad of
10.1
to obtain the horizontal double
monad
(S,\widehat{m},\widehat{e})
.
∎

We are now ready to recall the definition of categorical and coloured symmetric sequences.

Definition 10.4

(Categorical and coloured symmetric sequences)
.

•

Let
X
and
Y
be small
\mathcal{V}
-categories. A
categorical symmetric sequence

M\colon X\rightsquigarrow Y
is a profunctor
M\colon X\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow SY
,
i.e.
a
\mathcal{V}
-functor
M\colon SY^{\mathrm{op}}\times X\to\mathcal{V}
.

•

Let
X
and
Y
be sets. A
coloured symmetric sequence

M\colon X\rightsquigarrow Y
is a categorical symmetric
sequence from
X
to
Y
, considered as discrete
\mathcal{V}
-categories.

Categorical symmetric sequences and coloured symmetric sequences are the horizontal
1
-cells of double categories that we denote
\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}
and

\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}_{\mathcal{V}}
, which we may now obtain by forming the horizontal Kleisli double category (
9.1
) of the horizontal double monad
S\colon\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
.

Theorem 10.5
.

(1)

There exists a double category
\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}
having small
\mathcal{V}
-categories as objects,
\mathcal{V}
-functors as vertical 1-cells
and
categorical symmetric sequences as horizontal 1-cells.

(2)

There exists a double subcategory
\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}_{\mathcal{V}}
having sets as objects, functions as vertical 1-cells and coloured symmetric
sequences
as horizontal 1-cells.

Proof.

For
10.5
1
, it suffices that we apply
9.1
to the horizontal double monad
(S,\widehat{m},\widehat{e})\colon\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}\to\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
of
10.3
, where
m
and
e
are as in
Eq.

68
.
Indeed, a categorical symmetric sequence
M\colon X\rightsquigarrow Y
is
precisely a horizontal Kleisli 1-cell, and so by
Eq.

59
,
the composition of categorical symmetric sequences
M\colon X\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow SY
and
N\colon Y\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow SZ
is the profunctor
N\circ_{\mathbb{K}\mathsf{l}}M\colon X\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow SZ
found as the
composite

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces SY}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces SSZ}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces SZ\mathrlap{.}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces SN}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{m}_{Z}}

Using
Eqs.

8
,
11
and
67
, this composite has value at
\vec{z}=(z_{1},\dots,z_{m})\in SZ
and
x\in X

given by

(N\circ_{{\mathbb{K}\mathsf{l}}}M)(\vec{z},x)=\int^{\vec{w}\in SSZ,\vec{y}\in SY}SZ[\vec{z},\bigotimes_{i}\vec{w}^{i}]\times SN(\vec{w},\vec{y})\times M(\vec{y},x)

which by applying
Eq.

69
simplifies
to the following well-known formula (c.f.
[
FGHW08
, eq. (10)]
):

(N\circ_{{\mathbb{K}\mathsf{l}}}M)(\vec{z},x)=\int^{\vec{w}^{1},\dots,\vec{w}^{m}\in SZ,\vec{y}\in SY}SZ[\vec{z},\bigotimes_{i}\vec{w}^{i}]\times\bigsqcap_{1\leqslant i\leqslant m}N(\vec{w}^{i},y_{i})\times M(\vec{y},x)

which is a generalisation of the substitution monoidal structure for symmetric sequences
[
Kel05
]
.
10.5
2
follows
immediately and the formula for composition does not actually simplify significantly, since
SY
and
SZ
are genuine categories even
when
Y
and
Z
are sets.
∎

Remark 10.6
.

Even if the primary focus of our interest is the double category of coloured symmetric sequences
\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}_{\mathcal{V}}
, it is useful to consider the larger double
category of categorical symmetric sequences
\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}
. The reason is that the latter arises naturally from the double category of profunctors as a
Kleisli double
category and enjoys better closure properties than the former, since the free symmetric strict monoidal category on a discrete
\mathcal{V}
-category is
not discrete.

We now wish to apply the theory developed in the previous sections in order to obtain the desired oplax monoidal structures on
\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}
and
\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}_{\mathcal{V}}
. First note that, by
4.7
, the double category
\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
has a monoidal structure induced
from that on
\mathcal{V}
.
Thus, by
9.7
, it suffices to show that the vertical double monad
S\colon\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
has
well-behaved pseudomonoidal structure.

The key fact which allows us to do this is that, as a 2-monad on
\mathsf{Cat}_{\mathcal{V}}
,
S
is pseudomonoidal
[
HP02
,
Kel74
]
.
Indeed,
[
HP02
, Section 3.3]
shows that
S
can be equipped with the structure of a pseudo-commutative 2-monad,
while
[
HP02
, Theorem 7]
states that every pseudo-commutative 2-monad is pseudomonoidal,

cf.
also
[
Koc72
, Theorem 2.3]
. For our purposes, it will be convenient to describe the relevant structure explicitly.
First of all,
S
admits a
strength

[
Koc72
]
given by:

(74)

\displaystyle\kappa\colon X\times SY

\displaystyle\rightarrow S(X\times Y)

\displaystyle(x,\vec{y})

\displaystyle\mapsto\bigl((x,y_{1}),\dots,(x,y_{n})\bigr)\mathrlap{,}

as well as a
costrength

\kappa^{\prime}\colon SX\times Y\rightarrow S(X\times Y)
given dually. Note that, because the formula
for
\kappa(x,\vec{y})
repeats the variable
x
, we can only make the assignment of
Eq.

74

\mathcal{V}
-functorial when
\mathcal{V}
is

cartesian
monoidal—and this explains why we made this restriction in the first place. In this situation, the 2-functor

S
acquires
two
canonical lax monoidal structures built from the strength, the costrength and the monad multiplication as
in
[
Koc72
, eqs. (2.1) and (2.2)]
. In our case, one of
these lax monoidal structures has
S^{0}\colon 1\rightarrow S1
given by the monad unit, and
S^{2}_{X,Y}\colon SX\times SY\to S(X\times Y)
defined by lexicographic product:

(75)

\bigl((x_{1},\dots,x_{m})\,,\,(y_{1},\dots,y_{n})\bigr)\quad\mapsto\quad\bigl((x_{1},y_{1}),(x_{1},y_{2}),\dots,(x_{1},y_{n}),(x_{2},y_{1}),\dots,(x_{m},y_{n})\bigr)\mathrlap{,}

which we sometimes also denote by
\vec{x}\boxtimes\vec{y}
as in

Eq.

5
. The other lax monoidal structure has
the same
S^{0}
and binary constraints

SX\times SY\rightarrow S(X\times Y)
given by
colexicographic
product. Evidently, these two lax monoidal structures
are isomorphic, and this is the key aspect of
S
being pseudo-commutative in the sense of
[
HP02
]
.

In this situation, by
[
HP02
, Theorem 7]
, which is a higher-dimensional adaptation of
[
Koc72
, Theorem 2.3]
,
S

becomes a pseudomonoidal
2
-monad with respect to the lax monoidal structure
S^{2}
. It is not hard to see that the monad unit
e\colon 1\Rightarrow S
is in fact a genuine monoidal transformation;
however, the multiplication
m\colon SS\Rightarrow S

is not monoidal, but only a
pseudomonoidal
transformation; which is to say that the two sides of
the diagram

(76)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces SSX\times SSY}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S(SX\times SY)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces SS(X\times Y)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces SX\times SY}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S(X\times Y)\mathrlap{.}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces m_{X}\times m_{Y}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S^{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow m^{2}_{X,Y}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S(S^{2})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces m_{X\times Y}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S^{2}}

are not equal, but only coherently isomorphic via a
2
-cell as displayed. We now describe this
2
-cell
m^{2}_{X,Y}
explicitly. To this end, let us
take a typical element of
SSX\times SSY
, say

\bigl((\vec{x}^{1},\ldots,\vec{x}^{k}),(\vec{y}^{1},\ldots\vec{y}^{\ell})\bigr)

where
\vec{x}^{i}=(x^{i}_{1},\ldots,x^{i}_{m_{i}})
for
1\leq i\leq k

and
\vec{y}^{j}=(y^{j}_{1},\ldots,y^{j}_{n_{j}})
for
1\leq j\leq\ell
.
On the one hand, around the lower side of
Eq.

76
, this element is
sent first to
\big((x^{1}_{1},\dots,x^{k}_{m_{k}}),(y^{1}_{1},\dots,y^{\ell}_{n_{\ell}})\big)
and then to

\big((x^{1}_{1},y^{1}_{1}),(x^{1}_{1},y^{1}_{2}),\dots,(x^{1}_{1},y^{\ell}_{n_{\ell}}),(x^{1}_{2},y^{1}_{1}),\dots,(x^{1}_{2},y^{\ell}_{n_{\ell}}),\dots,(x^{k}_{m_{k}},y^{\ell}_{n_{\ell}})\big)\mathrlap{.}

This is the lexicographic order on four indices.
On the other hand, around the upper side of
Eq.

76
we obtain first
\bigl((\vec{x}^{1},\vec{y}^{1}),(\vec{x}^{1},\vec{y}^{2}),\dots,(\vec{x}^{k},\vec{y}^{\ell})\bigr)

and then, applying (
75
) to each pair, we get

\Bigl(\!\bigl((x^{1}_{1},y^{1}_{1}),(x^{1}_{1},y^{1}_{2}),\dots,(x^{1}_{m_{1}},y^{1}_{n_{1}})\bigr),\bigl((x^{1}_{1},y^{2}_{1}),(x^{1}_{1},y^{2}_{2}),\dots,(x^{1}_{m_{1}},y^{2}_{n_{2}})\bigr),\dots,\bigl((x^{k}_{1},y^{\ell}_{1}),(x^{k}_{1},y^{\ell}_{2}),\dots,(x^{k}_{m_{k}},y^{\ell}_{n_{\ell}})\bigr)\!\Bigr)

and so finally

\bigl((x^{1}_{1},y^{1}_{1}),(x^{1}_{1},y^{1}_{2}),\dots,(x^{1}_{m_{1}},y^{1}_{n_{1}}),(x^{1}_{1},y^{2}_{1}),\dots,(x^{1}_{m_{1}},y^{2}_{n_{2}}),\dots,(x^{k}_{m_{k}},y^{\ell}_{n_{\ell}})\bigr)\hbox to0.0pt{ .\hss}

This is a twisted lexicographic order on the indices, with the
significance order being
1
–
3
–
2
–
4
rather than

1
–
2
–
3
–
4
.
Clearly, there is a unique bijection
\theta
which exchanges these
orderings, giving the components of the desired natural isomorphism
m^{2}_{X,Y}
filling
Eq.

76
. This establishes the binary pseudomonoidality of
m
; the corresponding nullary pseudomonoidality constraint
m^{0}
is in fact the
identity
. That these data satisfy the necessary coherences to form a pseudomonoidal monad is now asserted in
[
HP02
, Theorem 7]
, but one could also establish this
directly, following a reasoning similar to that used in
[
HP02
, Section 3.3]
to establish pseudocommutativity.

The next lemma extends the pseudomonoidal structure of the
2-monad
S\colon\mathsf{Cat}_{\mathcal{V}}\to\mathsf{Cat}_{\mathcal{V}}
to a pseudomonoidal structure in the sense of
8.3
on the
vertical double monad
S\colon\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}\to\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
of
10.1
.
Before doing this, let us note that under our assumption that
\mathcal{V}
is cartesian monoidal, the induced monoidal structure on
\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
is also cartesian, in the sense that the ordinary monoidal structures on
(\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}})_{0}
and
(\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}})_{1}
that underlie it are both cartesian monoidal; as such, we will continue to write
\times
rather than
\otimes
for this tensor product, in particular, for its action on horizontal
1
-cells of
\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
.

Lemma 10.7
.

The vertical double monad
S\colon\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}\to\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
is
pseudomonoidal.

Proof.

We need to check that
S
is a lax monoidal double functor as in
5.1

and that
m
and
e
are pseudomonoidal vertical transformations as in
5.3
.
Let us begin by showing that
S
admits a lax monoidal structure. For
X_{1},X_{2}\in\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
,
the vertical 1-cells
S^{2}_{X_{1},X_{2}}\colon SX_{1}\times SX_{2}\to S(X_{1}\times X_{2})
and
S^{0}\colon 1\to S1

are given in (
75
). For
M_{1}\colon X_{1}\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow Y_{1}
and
M_{2}\colon X_{2}\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow Y_{2}
, the squares

(77)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces SX_{1}\times SX_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces SY_{1}\times SY_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S(X_{1}\times X_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S(Y_{1}\times Y_{2})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces SM_{1}\times SM_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S^{2}_{X_{1},X_{2}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow S^{2}_{M_{1},M_{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S^{2}_{Y_{1},Y_{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S(M_{1}\times M_{2})}

can be constructed following the same reasoning as in the proof of
10.1
,
i.e.
reducing to the cases where

M=\widehat{F}
,
N=\widehat{G}
and
M=\widecheck{F}
,
N=\widecheck{G}
, and using that
S
is lax monoidal
on
\mathsf{Cat}_{\mathcal{V}}
.

We already observed that the unit
e
is genuinely monoidal at the
2
-monad level, and the same is true for
e

qua
vertical transformation. As for the vertical transformation
m
, the axioms for a pseudomonoidal vertical transformation that concern only the vertical fragment
are exactly those expressing that
m
is a pseudomonoidal natural transformation in
\mathsf{Cat}_{\mathcal{V}}
, which we have discussed above. The only axiom
not of this form is
Eq.

40
, and this can be verified using the construction of the squares in (
77
)
via a
reduction to companions and conjoints and the modification axiom for the 2-cells filling (
76
).
∎

So
S
extends to a pseudomonoidal vertical double monad
S\colon\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
; and the last step required to establish
the normal oplax monoidal structure of coloured symmetric sequences is to
verify that this vertical double monad satisfies the additional conditions of
9.7
.

Lemma 10.8
.

The pseudomonoidal vertical double monad
S\colon\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
has the properties that:

(1)

The multiplication
m\colon SS\Rightarrow S
and unit
e\colon 1\Rightarrow S
are special
vertical
transformations.

(2)

The vertical 1-cells
S^{2}_{X,Y}\colon SX\times SY\to S(X\times Y)

and
S^{0}\colon 1\to S1
have companions.

(3)

The strength and costrength of
S
are special vertical transformations.

Proof.

Item

1
was already shown as part of
10.1
.

Item

2
is immediate since every vertical 1-cell in
\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
has a companion, see
2.8
.
For
Item

3
, the two cases are dual, so we only provide details for one. According
to
9.7
, the
strength in question is defined from the lax monoidal structure
S^{2}
of
S
via
Eq.

65
; but because we originally
obtained
S^{2}
using the strength
\kappa
of (
74
) and the dual costrength, it follows as in
[
Koc72
, Theorem 2.3]

that the strength of
Eq.

65
is this same
\kappa
, and similarly for the costrength. Thus, the condition we must prove
e.g.
for
the costrength is that,
for any
M\colon X\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow Y
and
N\colon W\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow Z
, the companion transpose
2
-morphism

(78)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces SX\times W}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces SY\times Z}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S(Y\times Z)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces SX\times W}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S(X\times W)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S(Y\times Z)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces SM\times N}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{\kappa}_{Y,Z}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptstyle\Downarrow{\widehat{\kappa}}_{M,N}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{\kappa}_{X,Z}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S(M\times N)}

is invertible.
To this end,
let
\vec{u}=\big((y_{1},z_{1}),\ldots,(y_{m},z_{m})\big)
in
S(Y\times Z)
and let
(\vec{x},w)\in SX\times W
where
\vec{x}=(x_{1},\dots,x_{m})
.
Note we assume that
\vec{u}
and
\vec{x}
have the same length; that we may do so without loss of generality will be clear from the formulae which follow.
Now, the profunctor along the bottom of
Eq.

78
has value at
(\vec{u},(\vec{x},w))
given by

\displaystyle S(M\times N)\big(\vec{u},\kappa(\vec{x},w)\big)

\displaystyle=\bigsqcup_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{m}}\bigsqcap_{1\leq i\leq m}(M\times N)\big(({y}_{\sigma(i)},z_{\sigma(i)}),(x_{i},w)\big)

\displaystyle=\bigsqcup_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{m}}\bigsqcap_{1\leq i\leq m}M(y_{\sigma(i)},x_{i})\times N(z_{\sigma(i)},w)\mathrlap{.}

On the other hand, the profunctor across the top of
Eq.

78
has value at
(\vec{u},(\vec{x},w))
given by

\displaystyle{}\phantom{\cong}{}\int^{\vec{v}\in SY,z^{\prime}\in Z}S(Y\times Z)[\vec{u},\kappa(\vec{v},z^{\prime})]\times(SM\times N)\bigl((\vec{v},z^{\prime}),(\vec{x},w)\bigr)

\displaystyle=\int^{\vec{v}\in SY,z^{\prime}\in Z}S(Y\times Z)[\vec{u},\kappa(\vec{v},z^{\prime})]\times SM(\vec{v},\vec{x})\times N(z^{\prime},w)

\displaystyle\cong\int^{v_{1},\dots,v_{m}\in Y,z^{\prime}\in Z}S(Y\times Z)[\vec{u},\kappa(\vec{v},z^{\prime})]\times\bigsqcap_{1\leqslant i\leqslant m}M(v_{i},x_{i})\times N(z^{\prime},w)

\displaystyle\cong\bigsqcup_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{m}}\int^{v_{1},\dots,v_{m}\in Y,z^{\prime}\in Z}\bigsqcap_{1\leqslant i\leqslant m}(Y\times Z)[(y_{\sigma(i)},z_{\sigma(i)}),(v_{i},z^{\prime})]\times\bigsqcap_{1\leqslant i\leqslant m}M(v_{i},x_{i})\times N(z^{\prime},w)

\displaystyle\cong\bigsqcup_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{m}}\int^{v_{1},\dots,v_{m}\in Y,z^{\prime}\in Z}\bigsqcap_{1\leqslant i\leqslant m}Y[y_{\sigma(i)},v_{i}]\times Z[z_{\sigma(i)},z^{\prime}]\times\bigsqcap_{1\leqslant i\leqslant m}M(v_{i},x_{i})\times N(z^{\prime},w)

\displaystyle\cong\bigsqcup_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{m}}\bigsqcap_{1\leqslant i\leqslant m}M(y_{\sigma(i)},x_{i})\times N(z_{\sigma(i)},w)\hbox to0.0pt{ ,\hss}

where at the first isomorphism we use (
69
) and at the
final one we use the Yoneda lemma.
By tracing it through we may see that the isomorphism constructed in this way is exactly
{\widehat{\kappa}}_{M,N}
, which is thus invertible.
As noted above, the specialness of the costrength follows by an
identical dual argument.
∎

Theorem 10.9
.

The double category
\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}
of categorical symmetric sequences admits a normal oplax monoidal structure,
given by arithmetic product of categorical symmetric sequences. Moreover, this restricts to a normal oplax monoidal
structure on the double category
\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}_{\mathcal{V}}
of coloured symmetric sequences.

Proof.

\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}
is the horizontal Kleisli double category of the
horizontal double monad induced by the vertical double monad
S\colon\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}\to\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
, as seen in the proof of
10.5
. Moreover, by
10.7
, the vertical double monad
S
is
pseudomonoidal, and by
10.8
, it satisfies the further hypotheses of
9.5
and
9.7
. Applying these results, we see that the monoidal structure of
\mathbb{P}\mathsf{rof}_{\mathcal{V}}
extends to a normal oplax monoidal structure on

\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}
, which clearly restricts back to the full sub-double-category
\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}_{\mathcal{V}}
.

It remains to show that the tensor product of horizontal
1
-cells computes the arithmetic product of categorical symmetric sequences. For categorical symmetric sequences
M_{1}\colon X_{1}\rightsquigarrow Y_{1}
and
M_{2}\colon X_{2}\rightsquigarrow Y_{2}
, the tensor product

M_{1}\boxtimes M_{2}\colon X_{1}\times X_{2}\rightsquigarrow Y_{1}\times Y_{2}
is defined as the profunctor:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{1}\times X_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces SY_{1}\times SY_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S(Y_{1}\times Y_{2})\mathrlap{.}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M_{1}\times M_{2}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{S^{2}_{\mathrlap{Y_{1},Y_{2}}}}\hskip 8.19447pt}

We now unfold this expression explicitly. First, by the definition of a companion in (
11
) applied to

S^{2}_{Y_{1},Y_{2}}
, the second of these profunctors is given by

\widehat{S^{2}_{\mathrlap{Y_{1},Y_{2}}}}\quad\;\;(\vec{y},(\vec{y}_{1},\vec{y}_{2}))=S(Y_{1}\times Y_{2})[\vec{y},\vec{y}_{1}\boxtimes\vec{y}_{2}]\mathrlap{,}

where
\vec{y}_{1}\boxtimes\vec{y}_{2}
is given by the lexicographic ordering
Eq.

75
.
Thus, using the definition of tensor product of profunctors (
26
) and of composition of profunctors
in (
8
), we obtain

(79)

(M_{1}\boxtimes M_{2})(\vec{y},(x_{1},x_{2}))=\int^{\vec{y}_{1},\vec{y}_{2}}S(Y_{1}\times Y_{2})[\vec{y},\vec{y}_{1}\boxtimes\vec{y}_{2}]\times M_{1}(\vec{y}_{1},x_{1})\times M_{2}(\vec{y}_{2},x_{2})\mathrlap{,}

which is the formula for the arithmetic product of categorical and coloured symmetric sequences and in particular gives
the formula in (
4
) for coloured symmetric sequences.
∎

The final step is to obtain the desired oplax monoidal structures at the level of bicategories rather than double categories. Indeed,
the horizontal bicategories of
\mathbb{C}\mathsf{atSym}_{\mathcal{V}}
and
\mathbb{S}\mathsf{ym}_{\mathcal{V}}
are the bicategories of categorical and
coloured symmetric sequences introduced in
[
FGHW18
]
for
\mathcal{V}=\mathsf{Set}
and in
[
GJ17
]
for a general
\mathcal{V}
. Thus, we can apply
9.9
to obtain:

Theorem 10.10
.

The bicategory of categorical symmetric sequences
\mathsf{CatSym}_{\mathcal{V}}
admits a normal oplax monoidal structure,
given by the arithmetic product of categorical symmetric sequences. Furthermore, this normal oplax monoidal
structure restricts to the bicategory of coloured symmetric sequences
\mathsf{Sym}_{\mathcal{V}}
.

Apart from its intrinsic interest, and the construction of an example of a sophisticated kind of low-dimensional categorical
structure by purely algebraic means, without any appeal to homotopy theory,
10.9
and

10.10
will be essential for
subsequent work on the Boardman–Vogt tensor product of bimodules between symmetric coloured operads, extending
that in
[
DH14
]
for bimodules between symmetric operads.

A.2.
Proof of
9.4

In this section, we illustrate the main ideas in the proof of
9.4
. We begin by stating a couple of technical lemmas which, along with
3.12
, are used repeatedly in the proof.

Lemma A.1
.

Let
F\colon\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{D}
be a double functor. For any horizontal
1
-cell
M\colon X\relbar\joinrel\mapstochar\joinrel\rightarrow Y
and vertical
1
-cell
f\colon Y\to Y^{\prime}
in

\mathbb{C}
, a 2-morphism in
\mathbb{D}
of the form on the left corresponds, under transpose
operations, to a 2-morphism of the form on the right

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces FX}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces FY^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces FX}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces FY}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces FY^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\bullet}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\bullet}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\bullet}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F(\widehat{f}\circ M)}

to coherence isomorphisms). Indeed,

We now provide a sample verification of one of the axioms needed in the proof of
9.4
. We will show that the left unit constraint of the monoidal structure of a Kleisli double category
{\mathbb{K}\mathsf{l}}(T)
for a monoidal
horizontal double monad is compatible with horizontal composition, namely the top left axiom of (
81
).

First of all, the left unit constraint
components
J\boxtimes M\Rightarrow M
as in
Eq.

61
bijectively correspond to cells

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I\otimes X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I\otimes TY}
